intro: 先輩 (senpai) means someone senior to you in the same school, club or workplace, such as an upperclassman or a coworker who joined before you. It is used both as a word and as a title after a name, like 田中先輩 (Tanaka-senpai). You hear it constantly in school anime and in the meme "notice me senpai."
literal: 先輩 is written with 先 (ahead, before) and 輩 (fellows, companions). Together they mean a fellow member who came before you.
usage: Senpai is about who joined a group first, not strictly about age. A student one year above you, a club member who joined earlier, or a coworker with more years at the company is your senpai.

In school and club settings, students call seniors 先輩 directly or add it to the family name: 鈴木先輩. At many companies, people address seniors by name + さん instead, but still use 先輩 when talking about them, as in 会社の先輩 (a senior at my company).
The opposite is 後輩 (kouhai). Senpai are expected to guide and look after their kouhai, and sometimes pay for meals. Kouhai are expected to show respect and use polite speech, at least at first.

In anime, a younger student calling someone 先輩 often hints at admiration or a crush, and English fan culture turned this into "notice me senpai." In real life the word has no romantic meaning. It just names a relationship, and it can be used broadly too, as in 人生の先輩 (someone with more life experience).

faq.q: What is the difference between senpai and sensei?
faq.a: 先輩 (senpai) is a senior in the same group as you, like an older student or a more experienced coworker. 先生 (sensei) is a teacher, doctor or other expert who teaches or serves you. Your senpai is a fellow member; your sensei is not.

faq.q: Is senpai romantic?
faq.a: No. In real life 先輩 just means a senior in your school, club or workplace. The romantic feel comes from anime and the English meme "notice me senpai."

faq.q: Can senpai be younger than you?
faq.a: Yes. Senpai depends on who joined first. At a company, someone younger who started before you can be your senpai, although age still matters in many situations.

intro: 後輩 (kouhai) means someone junior to you in the same school, club or workplace: an underclassman or a newer coworker. It is the opposite of 先輩 (senpai). You hear it in school and sports anime and in workplace dramas.
literal: 後輩 is written with 後 (after, behind) and 輩 (fellows, companions). Together they mean a fellow member who came after you.
usage: Like senpai, kouhai is about who joined a group later. First-year students are the kouhai of second- and third-year students, and new employees are the kouhai of people who joined the company earlier.
Unlike 先輩, 後輩 is not a title or a way to address someone. Nobody says "後輩！" or "田中後輩." Seniors call kouhai by name, often with くん, ちゃん or さん, or by family name with no suffix at all.
You use 後輩 when talking about someone: 部活の後輩 (a junior from my club) or 会社の後輩 (a junior at my company). Senpai often teach kouhai, help them settle in and sometimes treat them to meals.
In anime, the relationship is often played up, with kouhai who follow a senior everywhere. In real life it is a normal, everyday word that describes the relationship without any special feeling.

forms.note: The opposite of kouhai, and also usable as a title.

faq.q: Can you call someone kouhai?
faq.a: Not to their face. 後輩 is only used to talk about someone. To address a junior, use their name, usually with くん, ちゃん or さん.

faq.q: What is the difference between senpai and kouhai?
faq.a: 先輩 (senpai) joined the group before you, and 後輩 (kouhai) joined after you. Senpai can be used as a title, like 田中先輩, but kouhai cannot.

intro: 先生 (sensei) means "teacher." It is also a respectful title for doctors, lawyers, politicians, authors, manga artists and other experts. You hear it in school anime when students call their teacher, and in hospitals and martial arts schools.
literal: 先生 is written with 先 (before, ahead) and 生 (life, to be born). Read literally, the parts suggest someone born before you, meaning a person who came earlier and knows more.
usage: Students call their teacher 先生 directly, or add it to the family name: 山田先生. It works as both "you" and a title, so students almost never say あなた to a teacher.

It is not only for school teachers. Patients call doctors 先生, and the word is also used for dentists, lawyers, politicians, novelists, manga artists, and teachers of piano, calligraphy or martial arts.

Do not use 先生 for your own job. To say you are a teacher, say 教師です (kyoushi desu) or 英語を教えています (I teach English). The exception is teachers of small children, who often call themselves 先生 when talking to their students, as in 先生の話を聞いてね (listen to me).
In English, "sensei" usually means a martial arts teacher, but in Japanese it is much broader. People also sometimes call a friend 先生 as a joke when that friend is acting like an expert.

faq.q: Can I call myself sensei?
faq.a: Usually no. Calling yourself 先生 sounds self-important. Say 教師です or 英語を教えています instead. Teachers of young children are an exception and often refer to themselves as 先生 in class.

faq.q: Is sensei only for teachers?
faq.a: No. Doctors, lawyers, politicians, authors, manga artists and instructors of many skills are also called 先生.

faq.q: What is the difference between sensei and senpai?
faq.a: 先生 is a teacher or expert. 先輩 is a senior member of your own school, club or workplace.

intro: ちゃん (chan) is a friendly, affectionate suffix added to names, like ゆきちゃん (Yuki-chan). It is used for children, close friends, girls, family members and pets, and gives the name a warm, cute feel. You hear it all the time in anime between friends and for younger characters.
literal: ちゃん is generally explained as a childlike, softened pronunciation of さん (san), the standard polite suffix.
usage: Use ちゃん for small children of any gender, close friends, and especially girls and young women you know well. Grandparents, pets and even favorite celebrities get it too.
Boys are called ちゃん as small children and sometimes by family or old friends later in life. For teenage boys and men, くん is more usual, and ちゃん can sound childish or teasing unless you are close.

Do not use ちゃん for your boss, teachers, older people you are not close to, or anyone in a business setting. It would sound overly familiar or rude. Adding ちゃん to your own name sounds very childish or deliberately cute.
ちゃん also attaches to nicknames and short names (みっちゃん for Michiko) and appears inside common words like 赤ちゃん (baby), お兄ちゃん (big brother) and おばあちゃん (grandma).

forms.note: Read akachan. The everyday word for a baby.

faq.q: Can you use chan for boys?
faq.a: Yes for small boys, and sometimes for men by close family or old friends. For teenage boys and adult men you are not close to, くん or さん is safer.

faq.q: Is it rude to call someone chan?
faq.a: It can be. ちゃん shows closeness, so using it with a superior, a stranger or someone older can sound overly familiar or disrespectful. When unsure, use さん.

faq.q: What is the difference between chan and kun?
faq.a: ちゃん is cute and affectionate and is used mostly for girls, children and close friends. くん is used mostly for boys and young men, or by seniors for juniors.

intro: くん (kun) is a name suffix used mainly for boys and young men, like たかしくん (Takashi-kun). It is friendly but sounds a little more grown-up than ちゃん. You hear it in school anime when classmates and teachers talk to boys.
literal: くん is written 君 in kanji, the same character as 君 (kimi, "you"). The kanji 君 originally meant "lord" or "ruler."
usage: Use くん for boys from childhood through their teens, and for young men among friends. Teachers often call male students family name + くん, such as 佐藤くん.
In workplaces, a boss or senior may call junior employees family name + くん. This shows the speaker is above the listener, so never use くん for someone senior to you.

Girls and women are sometimes called くん too, mostly by teachers or bosses, but it is less common. Many schools now use さん for all students. In the Japanese parliament, members are formally called name + 君 regardless of gender.
Do not put くん on your own name. With adult men you do not know well, use さん instead.

forms.note: Often written this way in formal or older texts, like 田中君.
Read kun-zuke.

faq.q: Can girls be called kun?
faq.a: Sometimes. Teachers and bosses occasionally use くん for girls and women, but it is less common than for boys. ちゃん or さん is more typical.

faq.q: Is kun rude?
faq.a: Not to people junior or equal to you. But くん shows you are on the same level or above, so using it for a superior or an older stranger is rude.

faq.q: What is the difference between kun and chan?
faq.a: くん is mostly for boys and young men and feels a bit more grown-up. ちゃん is cuter and more affectionate, used mostly for girls, children and close friends.

intro: さん (san) is the standard polite suffix placed after a person's name, like 田中さん (Tanaka-san). It works like "Mr." or "Ms." but is used for any gender, with family names or given names. It is the safest way to refer to people in Japanese.
literal: さん is usually explained as a softer, everyday sound change from 様 (sama), the more formal honorific suffix.
usage: Use さん with anyone you are not close to: coworkers, neighbors, classmates, customers and people you just met. It usually goes after the family name (田中さん). With friends you know a bit better, it often goes after the given name (ゆみさん).
Never use さん for yourself. When introducing yourself, say 田中です, not 田中さんです. In business, people also drop さん when talking about their own coworkers to someone outside the company.
さん also attaches to jobs and shops in friendly speech: 店員さん (shop clerk), お医者さん (doctor), 本屋さん (bookstore), パン屋さん (bakery).
Calling someone with no suffix at all, called 呼び捨て (yobisute), is only for close friends, family or juniors. If you are not sure which suffix to use, さん is almost always safe.

faq.q: Can you use san with first names?
faq.a: Yes. さん works with family names and given names. Family name + さん is the default with people you don't know well, and given name + さん is common among friends or when someone asks you to use their first name.

faq.q: Do you use san for yourself?
faq.a: No. Never add さん to your own name. Just say your name, as in スミスです.

faq.q: What is the difference between san and sama?
faq.a: さん is the everyday polite suffix. 様 (sama) is much more formal and is used for customers, in letters and emails, and for people of very high status.

intro: 様 (sama) is a very respectful suffix placed after a name, a step above さん. Businesses use it for customers, as in お客様 (okyakusama), and it is written on letters and emails. In anime it is often used for royalty, gods, or a master a character serves.
literal: On its own, 様 means "appearance" or "manner," as in 様子 (yousu, state or look). As a suffix after a name, it became a respectful way to refer to a person.
usage: 様 is standard in customer service and business. Staff call customers お客様, and names on envelopes, emails, reservations and clinic waiting lists are written as 田中様.
In everyday conversation, calling a friend or coworker ○○様 to their face sounds overly formal, sarcastic or joking. Use さん instead.
様 is also part of many fixed words: 神様 (god), 王様 (king), 皆様 (everyone, formal), and set phrases like お疲れ様 and ご馳走様.

In anime, servants and devoted followers call their master ○○様, and arrogant characters call themselves 俺様 (ore-sama, "my great self"). In real life this sounds dramatic or comedic. Never put 様 on your own name.

faq.q: What is the difference between san and sama?
faq.a: さん is the everyday polite suffix for almost anyone. 様 is much more formal and is used for customers, in letters and emails, and for people of very high status.

faq.q: Is it weird to call someone sama?
faq.a: In normal conversation, yes. Calling a friend ○○様 sounds formal, sarcastic or playful. It is normal only in business, writing, and customer service.

faq.q: What does ore-sama mean?
faq.a: 俺様 (ore-sama) combines 俺 (I, rough male) with 様. It means something like "my great self" and is used by arrogant characters in fiction, or as a joke.

intro: お兄ちゃん (onii-chan) means "big brother." Younger siblings use it to call their older brother, and it has a warm, childlike feel. It is very common in anime, and small children also use it for any young man.
literal: お兄ちゃん is made of お (polite prefix), 兄 (older brother) and ちゃん (affectionate suffix).
usage: In Japanese families, younger siblings usually do not call older siblings by name. They call them お兄ちゃん or お姉ちゃん. Parents often call the eldest son お兄ちゃん too, from the younger child's point of view.
Small children call young men in general お兄ちゃん, a bit like "mister" for a young guy. Some shopkeepers in casual places also call a young male customer お兄ちゃん or 兄ちゃん.

As they grow up, some people switch to 兄ちゃん, 兄貴 (aniki) or the brother's name, while others, especially women, keep saying お兄ちゃん as adults. When talking about your brother to people outside the family, say 兄 (ani): 兄は大学生です (My older brother is a college student).
In anime, お兄ちゃん is often linked to a cute younger-sister character. In real life it is simply the normal family word for an older brother.

faq.q: What is the difference between onii-chan and oniisan?
faq.a: Both mean older brother. お兄ちゃん is more affectionate and childlike. お兄さん is more polite and grown-up, and is also used for someone else's brother or a young man you don't know.

faq.q: Can you call someone who isn't your brother onii-chan?
faq.a: Children often do, for any young man. Adults rarely do, except some casual shopkeepers. For a stranger, お兄さん is more polite.

faq.q: How do you say my older brother in Japanese?
faq.a: To people outside your family, say 兄 (ani). Inside the family, you call him お兄ちゃん, 兄ちゃん or his name.

intro: お姉ちゃん (onee-chan) means "big sister." Younger siblings use it to call their older sister, and it has a warm, childlike feel. It is common in anime, and small children also use it for any young woman.
literal: お姉ちゃん is made of お (polite prefix), 姉 (older sister) and ちゃん (affectionate suffix).
usage: In Japanese families, younger siblings usually call their older sister お姉ちゃん instead of her name. Parents often call the eldest daughter お姉ちゃん too, from the younger child's point of view.
Small children call young women in general お姉ちゃん, a bit like "miss." Many people keep calling their sister お姉ちゃん even as adults.
Be careful with strangers. When an adult man calls a young woman he does not know お姉ちゃん or ねえちゃん, it can sound overly familiar or crude. お姉さん is the more polite choice.
When talking about your own sister to people outside the family, say 姉 (ane): 姉は東京に住んでいます (My older sister lives in Tokyo).

forms.note: Read ane. Used when talking about your own sister to others.
Also used for someone else's sister or a young woman.

faq.q: What is the difference between onee-chan and oneesan?
faq.a: Both mean older sister. お姉ちゃん is more affectionate and childlike. お姉さん is more polite and is also used for someone else's sister or a young woman you don't know.

faq.q: Is it OK to call a stranger onee-chan?
faq.a: Children can. When an adult says it to a woman they don't know, it can sound overly familiar or crude. Use お姉さん or すみません instead.

intro: お兄さん (oniisan) means "older brother." It is more polite and grown-up than お兄ちゃん, and it is the normal way to talk about someone else's older brother. It is also used to call a young man you don't know, like a shop clerk or a guy on the street.
literal: お兄さん is made of お (polite prefix), 兄 (older brother) and さん (polite suffix).
usage: Use お兄さん for someone else's older brother: お兄さんはお元気ですか (How is your brother?). For your own brother, say 兄 (ani) when talking to others.
Some people call their own brother お兄さん, which sounds more formal or adult than お兄ちゃん. In anime, refined or polite characters often use it. A person may also call their spouse's older brother お兄さん.

It is used for young men in general. Children say お兄さん to a young man they don't know, and shop staff or street salespeople may call out to a male passerby with お兄さん. Calling a middle-aged man お兄さん can be a little flattering, while おじさん might offend.
Do not use it to address a coworker or a senior. Use their name + さん.

faq.a: Both mean older brother. お兄さん is more polite and is used for other people's brothers and young men in general. お兄ちゃん is the affectionate family word.

faq.q: Is it OK to call a stranger oniisan?
faq.a: Yes, in casual situations. Children, shop staff and people asking for help often use it for young men. In a more formal situation, すみません (excuse me) is safer.

intro: お姉さん (oneesan) means "older sister." It is more polite than お姉ちゃん and is the normal way to talk about someone else's older sister. It is also used for a young woman you don't know, such as a shop clerk, and in anime for a mature, big-sister type character.
literal: お姉さん is made of お (polite prefix), 姉 (older sister) and さん (polite suffix).
usage: Use お姉さん for someone else's older sister: お姉さんはどこに住んでいますか (Where does your sister live?). For your own sister, say 姉 (ane) when talking to others.
Some people call their own sister お姉さん, which sounds more formal than お姉ちゃん. A person may also call their spouse's older sister お姉さん.

It is often used for young women in general: 受付のお姉さん (the woman at reception), 店員のお姉さん (the shop clerk). Children call young women お姉さん too. Calling a woman おばさん can offend, so お姉さん is the safer and kinder word.
In anime and manga, お姉さんキャラ describes a calm, caring, older-sister type character. In real life it is just an everyday word.

faq.a: Both mean older sister. お姉さん is more polite and is used for other people's sisters and young women in general. お姉ちゃん is the affectionate family word.

faq.q: Is it polite to call a stranger oneesan?
faq.a: In casual situations, yes. It is friendly and flattering, and much safer than おばさん. In formal settings, すみません (excuse me) is better.

intro: お母さん (okaasan) means "mother" or "mom." Children use it to call their own mother, and it is also the polite word for someone else's mother. It is the most common way to say "mom" in Japanese.
literal: お母さん is made of お (polite prefix), 母 (mother) and さん (polite suffix).
usage: At home, children of all ages call their mother お母さん. Other choices are ママ (mostly small children, though some adults keep using it), 母さん (more casual, often used by sons) and おふくろ (used by adult men, mostly when talking about her).

When talking about your own mother to people outside the family, say 母 (haha): 母は看護師です (My mother is a nurse). Saying お母さん about your own mother in a formal setting, like a job interview, sounds childish.
For someone else's mother, say お母さん, or お母様 to be extra polite.
Parents often call each other お母さん and お父さん in front of their children, and some keep doing it even when the kids are not around. Teachers and doctors also call a child's mother お母さん.

forms.note: Read haha. Used when talking about your own mother to others.
Common with small children.
Read kaa-san. Often used by sons.

faq.q: What is the difference between okaasan and haha?
faq.a: Both mean mother. お母さん is what you call your mother and the polite word for someone else's mother. 母 (haha) is how you refer to your own mother when talking to people outside your family.

faq.q: Do Japanese people say mama?
faq.a: Yes. ママ is common with small children, and some people keep using it as adults. お母さん is the more standard choice for older children and adults.

intro: お父さん (otousan) means "father" or "dad." Children use it to call their own father, and it is also the polite word for someone else's father. It is the most common way to say "dad" in Japanese.
literal: お父さん is made of お (polite prefix), 父 (father) and さん (polite suffix).
usage: At home, children of all ages call their father お父さん. Other choices are パパ (mostly small children), 父さん (more casual, often used by sons) and 親父 (oyaji, used by adult men, mostly when talking about him).
When talking about your own father to people outside the family, say 父 (chichi): 父は会社員です (My father works for a company). Saying お父さん about your own father in a formal setting sounds childish.
For someone else's father, say お父さん, or お父様 to be extra polite.
Parents often call each other お父さん and お母さん in front of their children. Shop staff may also call a middle-aged man お父さん in a friendly way, though not everyone likes it.

forms.note: Read chichi. Used when talking about your own father to others.
Common with small children.
Read tou-san. Often used by sons.
Read otousama. For someone else's father.

faq.q: What is the difference between otousan and chichi?
faq.a: Both mean father. お父さん is what you call your father and the polite word for someone else's father. 父 (chichi) is how you refer to your own father when talking to people outside your family.

faq.q: What does oyaji mean?
faq.a: 親父 (oyaji) is a rough, casual word for father, mostly used by adult men when talking about their own dad. It can also mean a middle-aged man in general.

intro: おばあさん (obaasan) means "grandmother." It is also a polite way to refer to any elderly woman, the way English speakers might say "the old lady." You hear it in family conversations, folk tales and anime, often in its warmer form おばあちゃん (obaachan).
literal: おばあさん is made of お (a polite prefix), ばあ (a word for an old woman, related to the older word ばば) and さん (the polite name suffix). In kanji it can be written お祖母さん when it means your grandmother, but kana is far more common.
usage: Use おばあさん for someone else's grandmother or for an elderly woman you don't know. Children and adults alike use it to talk about older women in a neutral, polite way.
Inside the family, people usually call their own grandmother おばあちゃん, which sounds warm and affectionate. When talking about your own grandmother to others in polite speech, use 祖母 (sobo).

The long vowel matters. おばあさん (obaasan) is a grandmother or old woman, while おばさん (obasan) is an aunt or a middle-aged woman. Mixing them up can make someone sound decades older than they are, which may offend.
Calling a woman you don't know おばあさん to her face can feel blunt if she does not see herself as old. Staff in shops and hospitals often use the person's name with 様 or さん instead.

forms.note: Warm and casual. How most people address their own grandmother.
Read そぼ. Humble word for your own grandmother when speaking politely.
The male counterpart, also with a long vowel.

Talking about something that happened on the train

faq.q: What is the difference between obasan and obaasan?
faq.a: おばあさん (obaasan), with a long "aa", means grandmother or elderly woman. おばさん (obasan), with a short "a", means aunt or middle-aged woman. Saying the wrong one can be awkward, so hold the long vowel clearly.

faq.q: What is the difference between obaasan and obaachan?
faq.a: Both mean grandmother. おばあちゃん (obaachan) is warmer and more casual, and it is what most people call their own grandmother. おばあさん is a little more neutral and polite.

intro: おじさん (ojisan) means "uncle." It is also the everyday word for a middle-aged man, similar to "mister" when a child speaks to one. You hear it in family talk, from kids on the street, and from men in their 40s and 50s describing themselves.
literal: おじさん is お (polite prefix) + じ (an old word for uncle) + さん (polite suffix). When it means a family uncle it can be written 叔父さん (a parent's younger brother) or 伯父さん (a parent's older brother), but in everyday writing kana is common.
usage: For a family member, おじさん is your uncle or someone else's uncle. Many people call their own uncle おじさん or おじちゃん, sometimes with the uncle's first name added.
Children call any adult man they don't know おじさん, like "mister." Adults also use it to describe a man who looks middle-aged, as in あのおじさん (that guy over there).

Many men call themselves おじさん in a self-deprecating way once they feel older. Calling a man おじさん who feels young can sting, so younger-looking men are often called お兄さん instead, for example by shop staff.
Don't confuse it with おじいさん (ojiisan), which has a long "ii" and means grandfather or elderly man.

forms.note: Used by children and in close families.
Note the long vowel. A completely different age group.
Read おじさんくさい. Casual teasing for old-fashioned habits.

examples.context: Talking about a family visit
examples.romaji: Raishuu, ojisan ga Fukuoka kara kuru.
examples.en: My uncle is coming from Fukuoka next week.

examples.en: Mister, can you get the ball for me?

examples.context: A man in his 40s joking about getting older
examples.romaji: Ore mo mou ojisan da na.
examples.en: I guess I'm a middle-aged guy now too.

faq.q: What is the difference between ojisan and ojiisan?
faq.a: おじさん (ojisan) means uncle or middle-aged man. おじいさん (ojiisan), with a long "ii", means grandfather or elderly man. The vowel length changes the meaning, so say the long "ii" clearly.

faq.q: Is it rude to call someone ojisan?
faq.a: It is not a rude word, and children use it all the time. But many men in their 30s or 40s don't like hearing it from adults, because it means they look middle-aged. If unsure, use their name with さん.

intro: おばさん (obasan) means "aunt." It is also the everyday word for a middle-aged woman, a bit like "ma'am" or "lady" when a child says it. You hear it in family talk, from children, and from women joking about their own age.
literal: おばさん is お (polite prefix) + ば (an old word for aunt) + さん (polite suffix). When it means a family aunt it can be written 叔母さん (a parent's younger sister) or 伯母さん (a parent's older sister), but kana is common.
usage: For a family member, おばさん is your aunt or someone else's aunt. Children often say おばちゃん, which is warmer.
Children call adult women they don't know おばさん, and people use it for women who look middle-aged, as in 隣のおばさん (the lady next door).

Be careful with adults. Many women in their 30s or 40s feel hurt if a stranger calls them おばさん, because it says they look older. Shop staff and polite speakers usually say お姉さん or use the person's name with さん instead.
Don't confuse it with おばあさん (obaasan), which has a long "aa" and means grandmother or elderly woman.

forms.note: Friendly and casual. Common in the Kansai region for any older woman.
Note the long vowel. A different age group.
Both read おば. Plain words for your own aunt when speaking politely.

examples.romaji: Watashi mo mou obasan da kara ne.
examples.en: Well, I'm middle-aged now too, you know.

faq.q: Is obasan rude?
faq.a: The word itself is not rude, and it is normal for your aunt or from a child. But calling an adult woman you don't know おばさん can offend, because it labels her as middle-aged. お姉さん or her name with さん is safer.

faq.q: What is the difference between obasan and obaasan?
faq.a: おばさん (obasan) means aunt or middle-aged woman. おばあさん (obaasan), with a long "aa", means grandmother or elderly woman.

intro: 友達 (tomodachi) means "friend" or "friends." It is the standard everyday word for a friend, used by kids and adults alike. You hear it in phrases like 友達になろう ("Let's be friends").
literal: 友達 is written with 友 (friend) and 達 (a plural suffix, as in 私達, "we"). Even though 達 marks a group, 友達 now works for one friend or many.
usage: 友達 is neutral and works in almost any situation, from chatting with classmates to telling a coworker what you did on the weekend.
Japanese usually does not mark singular or plural, so 友達と映画を見た can mean "I saw a movie with a friend" or "with friends." Add 一人 or a number if it matters.
In formal writing or speeches, people often use 友人 (yuujin) instead, which sounds more adult and polite. For a best friend, use 親友 (shinyuu).
Saying ただの友達 ("just a friend") is the common way to say there is nothing romantic between two people.

forms.note: Casual and friendly.
Read しんゆう. For someone you are very close to.
Read ゆうじん. Used in writing, speeches and polite speech.
Read とも. Common in songs and as part of compounds.

faq.q: Is tomodachi singular or plural?
faq.a: It can be either. 友達 originally had a plural suffix, but today it means one friend or several. Context or a number tells you which.

faq.q: What is the difference between tomodachi and nakama?
faq.a: 友達 (tomodachi) is a friend in general. 仲間 (nakama) is someone you belong to a group with or share a goal with, like teammates, coworkers or a crew. A nakama is not always a close friend.

faq.q: How do you say best friend in Japanese?
faq.a: The usual word is 親友 (shinyuu). Young people also say ズッ友 (zuttomo, "friends forever") as slang.

intro: 仲間 (nakama) means "companions" or "comrades": people who belong to the same group or work toward the same goal. In anime it is the crew or team the hero fights for. In daily life it covers teammates, coworkers and people who share a hobby.
literal: 仲間 is written with 仲 (relations between people) and 間 (between, space). Together they describe the people you are connected to within a group.
usage: 仲間 focuses on belonging together, not on how close you are. 仕事仲間 means people you work with, 飲み仲間 means drinking buddies, and バンド仲間 means bandmates.

In anime and manga, 仲間 carries a strong feeling of loyalty: the people you would risk everything for. Real-life use is calmer. Saying 仲間 in everyday speech sounds natural, but long speeches about 仲間 can feel dramatic.
仲間 is also used for categories of things, in the sense of "the same kind." イルカはクジラの仲間 means dolphins belong to the whale family.
The phrase 仲間外れ (nakama hazure) means being left out of a group, and 仲間に入れて means "Can I join you?"

forms.note: Stresses several people.
Read なかまはずれ. Often about children leaving someone out.
Read なかまにいれて. Casual, often said by children.

faq.q: What does nakama mean in anime?
faq.a: It means the companions or crew a character belongs to. Anime often use it with a strong sense of loyalty, as in protecting your 仲間 no matter what.

faq.q: What is the difference between nakama and tomodachi?
faq.a: 友達 (tomodachi) is a friend in general. 仲間 (nakama) is someone in your group or on your side, like teammates or coworkers. You can be nakama without being close friends.

intro: お前 (omae) means "you," but in a rough, very casual way. Men use it with close friends and people below them, and anime characters use it constantly. With anyone you are not close to, it sounds rude.
literal: お前 is お (polite prefix) + 前 (front). It once referred politely to the person in front of you, but over time it lost its respect and became a casual or even condescending way to say "you."
usage: Among close male friends, お前 is normal and shows familiarity. Parents sometimes use it with their children, and older people with much younger family members.

Used toward a stranger, a customer, a teacher or a boss, お前 is clearly rude. It sounds like talking down to them or starting a fight. It is not as hostile as 貴様 (kisama) or てめえ, but it is far from polite.
Some husbands call their wives お前. This is old-fashioned, and many people today find it disrespectful.
Anime use お前 much more than real life does. Learners should avoid it until they know someone well, and instead use the person's name with さん. Women use it less, though some do with close friends.

forms.note: Read おまえら. Plural, very casual.
A slurred, tougher version heard in tough-guy speech and some dialects.
More neutral, though Japanese speakers often avoid saying "you" at all.

faq.q: Is omae rude?
faq.a: Yes, unless you are very close to the person. Between close friends it is normal, but said to a stranger, a teacher or a boss it is rude and can sound like you are picking a fight.

faq.q: What is the difference between omae and kisama?
faq.a: Both are rough ways to say "you." お前 is casual and can be friendly between close friends. 貴様 (kisama) is hostile and insulting in modern speech, and is mostly heard in anime and dramas.

faq.q: What does omae wa mou shindeiru mean?
faq.a: お前はもう死んでいる means "You are already dead." It is a famous anime line and a meme, not something people say in normal conversation.

intro: あなた (anata) means "you." It is the word textbooks teach first, and you see it in songs, ads and surveys. In real conversation, though, Japanese speakers usually avoid it and use the person's name instead.
literal: あなた originally meant "over there" or "that far side," a direction word. Over time it came to point to a person. It is sometimes written 貴方 in kanji, but kana is far more common.
usage: あなた is grammatically neutral, but saying it to someone's face can sound distant or a little cold. With people you know, use their name with さん, or simply leave "you" out; Japanese often drops it.
It is natural in writing addressed to anyone: surveys, ads, instructions and song lyrics. あなたの好きな食べ物は何ですか ("What is your favorite food?") on a form is normal.
Avoid あなた with teachers, bosses and customers. Using it to a superior sounds like you don't respect them. Use their title instead, like 先生 or 部長.
Some wives call their husbands あなた, like "dear." This is a bit old-fashioned but still heard, especially in TV dramas. In arguments, あなた can sound sharp.

forms.note: Neutral plural.
A shortened form. Can be friendly in some regions, but often sounds rude or pushy.
Read あなた. Seen in some writing and lyrics.

examples.context: A question on a survey form
examples.romaji: Anata no suki na tabemono wa nan desu ka?

examples.context: A wife calling a husband to dinner (a bit old-fashioned)

faq.q: Is anata rude?
faq.a: Not by itself, but it can sound cold or distant when said directly to someone, and it is rude toward a boss or teacher. Using the person's name with さん is usually better.

faq.q: Why don't Japanese people say anata?
faq.a: Japanese often leaves out "you" because context makes it clear. When people need to refer to you, they usually use your name or title. Saying あなた a lot can feel like you are keeping someone at arm's length.

faq.q: Does anata mean darling?
faq.a: It can. Some wives call their husbands あなた, similar to "dear." This use is a bit old-fashioned today.

intro: 君 (kimi) means "you." It is a casual word used mostly by men toward equals or people younger or lower in rank, and it is extremely common in song lyrics. Many readers know it from titles and lyrics like 君に会いたい ("I want to see you").
literal: The kanji 君 once meant a lord or ruler, as in 君主 (monarch). Over time it became a word for "you" between equals, and later toward people below the speaker. It is the same kanji as the name suffix くん (kun).
usage: Men often use 君 with friends, girlfriends or people younger than them. Teachers and bosses use it with students and junior employees, sometimes just as 君 to call someone over.
Never use 君 toward someone older or higher than you. It sounds like you are talking down to them.
In songs, poems and romantic lines, 君 is the standard "you." It sounds gentle and a little emotional there, which is why it appears in so many lyrics.
Like other words for "you," it is often better to use the person's name. Women use 君 less in speech, though they use it freely in lyrics and writing.

forms.note: Read きみたち. Often a teacher speaking to a class.
Read きみら. More casual plural.
Read くん. Same kanji, attached to names of boys and juniors.

faq.q: Is kimi rude?
faq.a: It is not rude between friends or toward juniors. But using 君 toward someone older or higher in rank, like a teacher or a boss, is rude because it talks down to them.

faq.q: What is the difference between kimi and anata?
faq.a: Both mean "you." 君 is more casual and often used by men toward equals or juniors, and it is common in songs. あなた is more neutral and common in writing. In conversation, both are often replaced by the person's name.

intro: 俺 (ore) means "I" or "me." It is a casual, masculine word that men and boys use with friends and family. It sounds confident and a bit rough, which is why many anime heroes use it.
literal: 俺 is simply a first-person pronoun. The kanji is used only for this word, and it is often written in kana as おれ or オレ.
usage: Most Japanese men use 俺 with friends, family and people their own age or younger. It sounds natural and relaxed in casual talk.
In formal settings, men switch. At work or in a job interview, they use 私 (watashi), and in semi-formal situations many use 僕 (boku). Saying 俺 to a client or in an interview sounds unprofessional.
俺 sounds more masculine and rougher than 僕. Women rarely use it in standard Japanese, though some do in certain dialects or as a deliberate style.
Anime characters who use 俺 are often tough, confident or hot-headed. A man using 俺 in real life is normal and does not mean they are tough; it is just casual.

forms.note: Read おれたち. Also 俺ら (おれら), more casual.
Read おれさま. Sounds boastful, mostly heard from arrogant characters or as a joke.
Read ぼく. Gentler and more polite.

examples.context: Friends making plans to go out
Spotting a friend picking up the wrong drink
Taking charge of a difficult situation

faq.q: Can girls use ore?
faq.a: Women rarely use 俺 in standard Japanese, and it sounds very masculine. Some women use it in certain dialects, and some anime characters use it to show a tomboyish style.

faq.q: What is the difference between ore and boku?
faq.a: Both are words men use for "I." 俺 is casual and sounds rougher and more masculine. 僕 is softer and a bit more polite. In formal situations, men usually use 私.

intro: 僕 (boku) means "I" or "me." It is mostly used by boys and men, and it sounds gentler and more polite than 俺 (ore). Adults also use ぼく to talk to little boys, like "little guy."
literal: The kanji 僕 originally meant "servant," as in 下僕 (geboku, servant). As a word for "I," it started out humble and today simply sounds soft and modest.
usage: Boys use 僕 from early childhood. Many men keep using it with people they are not close to, or in semi-formal situations, because it sounds polite but not stiff.
Some men use 僕 all the time, even with friends; it gives a gentle, polite image. Others switch to 俺 with friends and 僕 with teachers or older people.
In very formal settings, such as business meetings or interviews, men use 私 (watashi) instead.
Adults call a small boy ぼく, as in ぼく、何歳？ ("How old are you, little guy?"). Some girls and women use 僕 too, especially in anime and songs, where it gives a boyish feel.

forms.note: Read ぼくたち / ぼくら. 僕ら is common in songs.
Adults use it to address a young boy.
Read おれ. More casual and masculine.

examples.context: A student introducing themselves to the class
A child wanting a turn at a game
An adult asks a small boy his age
examples.en: How old are you, little guy?

faq.q: Can girls use boku?
faq.a: It is unusual in everyday speech, but some girls and women use it, and it often appears in anime and songs to give a boyish feel.

faq.q: Is boku polite?
faq.a: It is softer and more polite than 俺, and fine with teachers or people you just met. In formal business situations, though, men use 私 instead.

intro: 私 (watashi) means "I" or "me." It is the standard, neutral word for yourself, used by everyone in polite situations and by most women in daily life. It is usually the first Japanese word for "I" that learners study.
literal: The kanji 私 means "private" or "personal," as in 私立 (shiritsu, privately run). Read わたし, it means "I."
usage: 私 works in any polite situation: introductions, work, school and talking to strangers. Men use it at work and in formal settings, even if they say 俺 or 僕 with friends.
Women commonly use 私 in casual speech too. For a man, using 私 with close friends sounds a bit stiff.
For very formal occasions, such as speeches or speaking to important clients, people use わたくし (watakushi), written with the same kanji. Casual feminine speech often shortens it to あたし.
Japanese often leaves out "I" when it is clear, so repeating 私は in every sentence sounds unnatural. Use it when you introduce yourself or contrast yourself with others.

forms.note: Same kanji 私. Used in speeches and formal business.
A softer, casual version mostly used by women.
Read わたしたち. Neutral plural.

faq.q: Can men use watashi?
faq.a: Yes. Men use 私 at work, in interviews and with people they need to be polite to. With close friends, most men switch to 俺 or 僕.

faq.q: What is the difference between watashi, boku and ore?
faq.a: 私 is neutral and polite, used by everyone. 僕 is a softer word mostly used by men and boys. 俺 is casual and masculine, used among friends.

faq.q: What does watashi wa mean?
faq.a: 私は means "I" plus the topic marker は, so it starts a sentence about yourself, as in 私は学生です ("I am a student").

intro: 兄貴 (aniki) means "big brother" in a casual, masculine way, like "big bro." Men use it for their own older brother, and also for an older man they look up to. In anime and gangster films, it is how younger members address a senior in the group.
literal: 兄貴 is written with 兄 (older brother) and 貴 (noble, valuable). The 貴 part originally added respect, but today the word sounds casual and manly.
usage: Many men call their own older brother 兄貴, and use it when talking about that brother to friends, as in うちの兄貴 (my big brother). It sounds more rugged than お兄ちゃん.
兄貴 is also used for an older man someone admires, like a mentor at work or a senior in a group of friends. It shows respect and closeness at the same time.
In yakuza movies and anime, 兄貴 is what younger members call a senior member. Because of this image, using it for someone outside your family can sound tough or playful.
Women rarely use 兄貴 for their brothers; they usually say お兄ちゃん. In polite speech, say 兄 (ani) for your own brother and お兄さん for someone else's.

forms.note: Read あねき. The female counterpart, used the same way.
Read あに. Use in polite speech about your own brother.
Read おにいちゃん. Softer and common in families.

examples.context: Telling a friend about family
examples.romaji: Aniki wa ima, Nagoya de hataraite iru.
examples.en: My big brother is working in Nagoya now.

examples.context: A younger guy calling after an older one they look up to
Bragging about an older brother to friends
examples.romaji: Uchi no aniki, ryouri ga umain da.
examples.en: My big brother is a really good cook.

faq.q: What is the difference between aniki and onii-chan?
faq.a: Both mean big brother. 兄貴 sounds rough and manly and is mostly used by men. お兄ちゃん is softer and affectionate, used by younger children, sisters and families in general.

faq.q: Is aniki a yakuza word?
faq.a: It is a normal word for big brother, but in gangster films and anime, younger members call a senior member 兄貴. That is why it can sound tough when used outside the family.

intro: 妹 (imouto) means "younger sister." It is the normal word for talking about your own little sister. You also hear it in anime, where the little sister is a common character type.
literal: 妹 is written with 女 (woman) and 未. The kanji simply means younger sister. Japanese has separate words for older and younger siblings, so 妹 is only for a sister younger than you.
usage: Use 妹 when you talk about your own younger sister: 妹が一人います ("I have one younger sister").
For someone else's younger sister, add さん: 妹さん. This is the polite way to ask about another person's family.
You don't call your sister 妹 to their face. In Japanese families, older siblings call younger ones by their first name or a nickname.
In anime, 妹 often refers to the little sister character type. In real life it is just an everyday family word with no special nuance.

forms.note: Read いもうとさん. Polite, for someone else's sister.
Read あね. お姉さん for someone else's.
Read おとうと. The male counterpart.
Read しまい. Sisters as a group.

examples.en: I often fight with my little sister.

faq.q: How do you say older sister in Japanese?
faq.a: Your own older sister is 姉 (ane). Someone else's is お姉さん (oneesan), and many people call their own older sister お姉ちゃん (onee-chan).

faq.q: What is the difference between imouto and imouto-san?
faq.a: 妹 is your own younger sister. 妹さん adds respect and is used for someone else's younger sister.

intro: 何 (nani) means "what." Said alone as なに？！ it is a shocked "What?!", which is why it is so well known from anime. It is also the everyday question word in sentences like 何を食べる？ (What are you going to eat?).
literal: 何 is the kanji for "what." It is read なに (nani) or なん (nan) depending on the sound that comes after it.
usage: Alone, なに？ means "What?" It can be a real question, for example when someone calls your name, or a reaction of surprise. A sharp なに？！ or なにっ！ is the dramatic "What?!" you hear in anime.
Before です, だ, の and counters, 何 is usually read なん: 何ですか (nan desu ka, "What is it?"), 何時 (nanji, what time), 何人 (nannin, how many people). Before を and many other words it is なに: 何を (nani o).

Tone matters. A light なに？ to a friend is fine. Snapped at someone, or as なによ or なんだよ, it sounds irritated, like "What do you want?" With teachers, customers or strangers, answer a call with はい instead.
If you did not hear what someone said, a bare なに？ can sound blunt. In polite speech, say すみません、もう一度お願いします (Sorry, could you say that again?).

forms.note: Use with people you don't know well.
A different question word built on 何.
Said when someone asks what is wrong.
Casual, among friends.

Deciding what to order at a restaurant

faq.q: Is nani rude?
faq.a: Not by itself. It is a normal question word. A bare なに？ snapped at someone can sound rude, so with teachers, bosses or strangers use はい when called and 何ですか or 何でしょうか when asking.

faq.q: What is the difference between nani and nan?
faq.a: They are the same word, 何. It is read なん before sounds like d, t and n and before counters (何ですか, 何時), and なに in most other places (何を, なに？).

intro: すごい (sugoi) means "amazing," "awesome" or "incredible." People say it when something impresses them, from a friend's drawing to a great view. It is one of the most common reactions in anime and in everyday Japanese.
literal: すごい is an i-adjective. It can be written 凄い, but kana is far more common today. It once described something strikingly intense, even frightening, and later came to mean "amazing."
usage: Alone, すごい！ is "Wow!" or "Amazing!" Add ね (すごいね) to share the feeling with someone, or です to make it polite: すごいですね.
It also works like "really" or "very." The correct adverb form is すごく: すごく楽しい (really fun). In casual speech many people say すごい楽しい instead. This is very common but considered nonstandard.
In rough casual speech, especially among men and in anime, it becomes すげえ or すげー (sugee). This is fine with friends but too rough for a boss or a customer.
すごい can describe bad things too: すごい雨 is heavy rain and すごい渋滞 is terrible traffic. Also, telling a boss すごいですね can sound a little like you are grading them. Many people say さすがです in that situation.

forms.note: Safe with coworkers and people you just met.
The adverb form: すごくおいしい.
Mostly young men, among friends.
The past form.

examples.context: Looking at a friend's drawing
Talking about a concert last night
A coworker shows something they built
examples.romaji: Hitori de zenbu tsukutta n desu ka. Sugoi desu ne.
examples.en: You made all of this by yourself? That's amazing.

faq.q: What is the difference between sugoi and sugee?
faq.a: They are the same word. すげー (sugee) is a rough, casual way of saying すごい, used mostly by young men and in anime. すごい is fine in any setting.

faq.q: Is sugoi polite?
faq.a: すごい on its own is casual. Add です to make it polite: すごいですね (That's amazing). With a boss, さすがです is often a better compliment.

intro: やばい (yabai) is slang that means "dangerous" or "bad," but young people also use it to mean "amazing." Depending on the situation, やばい！ can mean "Oh no!" or "This is incredible!" You hear it constantly in anime, on TV and in casual talk.
literal: やばい is an i-adjective usually written in kana. It started as slang for something risky or dangerous. The positive "amazing" sense spread among young people in recent decades.
usage: The original meaning is negative: "dangerous," "risky" or "I'm in trouble." やばい、遅刻する！ means "Oh no, I'm going to be late!"
The newer meaning is positive: "amazing" or "insanely good." このラーメン、やばい usually means the ramen is incredible. Tone, facial expression and context tell you which meaning is intended.
It is slang. Use it with friends, not in a job interview, with a boss or with customers. Some older people find it crude. In rough casual speech it becomes やべえ or やべー.
やばくない？ ("Isn't that crazy?") is a common way to share a reaction, good or bad, with a friend.

forms.note: Very casual, mostly young men.

forms.en: It was crazy / That was close
forms.note: The past form.
Asks a friend to share the reaction.
Often used in writing for emphasis.

Looking at a price tag with a friend

faq.q: Is yabai a bad word?
faq.a: It is not a swear word, but it is slang. It is fine with friends and people your age. Avoid it at work, in interviews and with older people you need to be polite to.

faq.q: Does yabai mean good or bad?
faq.a: Both. It started out meaning "dangerous" or "bad," and young people now also use it for "amazing." The situation and tone make the meaning clear.

intro: マジ (maji) is casual slang for "seriously" or "for real." マジで？ means "Are you serious?" and マジで on its own means "Really, I mean it." It is very common among young people and in anime.
literal: マジ is generally understood to be short for 真面目 (majime, serious, earnest). It is usually written in katakana.
usage: As a question, マジ？ or マジで？ means "Seriously?" or "For real?" It is a reaction to surprising news.
As an adverb, マジで means "really" or "seriously": マジで疲れた (I'm seriously tired). People also put マジ directly before adjectives, as in マジうまい (really tasty).
マジか (majika), often said to yourself, means "No way..." or "You're kidding." マジかよ is a rougher version.
It is casual slang only. With teachers, customers or a boss, say 本当ですか (Really?) instead.

forms.note: The most common form, as a question or an adverb.
Often said to yourself.
Normally read ほんき, but manga often read it マジ.
Use this instead of マジ with people above you.

Coming home after a long day
Finding out the trains have stopped

faq.q: Is maji rude?
faq.a: It is not rude, but it is slang. Use it with friends. With a teacher or boss, 本当ですか is the right way to say "Really?"

faq.q: What is the difference between maji and hontou?
faq.a: Both can mean "really." 本当 (hontou) is a normal word you can use with anyone, and 本当ですか is polite. マジ is casual slang for friends.

intro: 嘘 (uso) means "a lie." As a reaction, うそ！ or うそでしょ！ means "No way!" or "You're kidding!", not a real accusation. You hear it all the time in anime and casual talk when someone gets shocking news.
literal: The kanji 嘘 is made of 口 (mouth) and 虚 (empty, false). In everyday writing people often just use kana: うそ.
usage: As a noun, 嘘 means a lie. 嘘をつく (uso o tsuku) means "to tell a lie."
As a reaction, うそ！, うそでしょ？ or a stretched うっそー mean "No way!" They show surprise and are not a claim that the other person is lying.
Be careful with 嘘つき (usotsuki, liar). That is a real accusation and can hurt. A serious, angry 嘘だ！ can also mean "That's a lie!"
うそ as a reaction is casual. To a boss or a customer it sounds too familiar and may sound like you doubt them, so say えっ、本当ですか (Oh, really?) instead.

forms.note: Casual reaction to shocking news.
The normal verb phrase.
A real accusation; can be hurtful.
Playful, stretched reaction.

A parent talking to a child

faq.q: Is saying uso rude?
faq.a: As a reaction, うそ！ just means "No way!" and is not rude among friends. It is too casual for a boss or customer. Calling someone 嘘つき (liar) is a real accusation.

faq.q: What does uso deshou mean?
faq.a: 嘘でしょう, often shortened to うそでしょ, means "You're kidding, right?" or "No way." It shows strong surprise or disbelief.

intro: 本当 (hontou) means "true" or "the truth." 本当？ asks "Really?" and 本当に means "truly" or "really." In casual speech it is often shortened to ほんと (honto).
literal: 本当 combines 本 (origin, true) and 当 (to hit, to be right). Together they mean "true" or "real."
usage: As a reaction, 本当？ or ほんと？ means "Really?" With people you need to be polite to, say 本当ですか.
本当に is an adverb meaning "truly" or "really": 本当にありがとう (thank you so much), 本当にごめん (I'm really sorry).
本当は means "actually" or "the truth is": 本当は行きたくない (Actually, I don't want to go).
Unlike マジ or うそ, 本当ですか is fine with anyone, including a boss. In the Kansai region you will also hear ほんま, the local word for 本当.

forms.note: Safe with anyone.
Strengthens thanks, apologies and adjectives.
Introduces what someone really thinks.
Very common in speech and texts.

faq.q: What is the difference between hontou and honto?
faq.a: They are the same word. ほんと (honto) is a shorter, casual way of saying 本当 (hontou) and is very common in speech and messages.

faq.q: What does hontou ni mean?
faq.a: 本当に means "truly" or "really." It makes words stronger, as in 本当にありがとう (thank you so much). Said alone as a question, 本当に？ means "Really?"

intro: なるほど (naruhodo) means "I see" or "That makes sense." People say it when they understand something new or are convinced by an explanation. You hear it in everyday conversation and in anime when a character finally gets it.
literal: なるほど can be written 成程, though this is rare today. 成 means "to become" or "to be achieved" and 程 means "degree" or "extent."
usage: Say なるほど when someone explains something and it clicks: "Ah, I see." It shows you understood and that the explanation makes sense to you.

With friends, なるほど or なるほどね is natural. In business, many Japanese people feel なるほど sounds like you are judging the other person's point, so saying it to a boss or a customer can come across as slightly rude. Use そうなんですね or おっしゃる通りです instead.
Saying なるほど、なるほど over and over can sound like you are not really listening.
You can also say it to yourself while thinking: なるほど、そういうことか (I see, so that's what it is).

forms.note: Natural with friends and family.
Safer with a boss or customer.

faq.q: Is naruhodo rude?
faq.a: Not with friends or classmates. In business, many people consider it slightly rude to say なるほど to a boss or customer, because it can sound like you are evaluating them. そうなんですね is safer.

faq.q: What is the difference between naruhodo and sou desu ka?
faq.a: なるほど means you understand and the explanation makes sense. そうですか (Oh, is that so?) just shows you heard new information.

meaning: That's right; well, let me see
intro: そうですね (sou desu ne) means "That's right" or "I agree." It is also a polite filler, like "Well, let me see...", when someone needs a moment to think. It is one of the most frequent phrases in polite Japanese conversation.
literal: そう means "so" or "like that," です is the polite "is," and ね is a particle asking for agreement, like "right?" Literally it is "It is so, isn't it."
usage: For agreement: when someone says いい天気ですね (Nice weather, isn't it?), you answer そうですね. It shows you share their view.
As a thinking filler: when asked a question, you can start with そうですね… to buy time, like "Hmm, let me see." People often stretch it to そうですねえ.
With friends it sounds a bit stiff. The casual forms are そうだね and the softer そうね.
Do not confuse it with そうですか (sou desu ka), which means "Oh, is that so?" and reacts to new information rather than agreeing.

forms.note: With friends and family.
Reacts to new information; not agreement.
Stretched out while thinking.
Sounds gentle; common among women.

faq.q: What is the difference between sou desu ne and sou desu ka?
faq.a: そうですね agrees with the other person ("That's right") or buys time to think. そうですか means "Oh, is that so?" and simply reacts to something new you just heard.

faq.q: How do you say sou desu ne casually?
faq.a: With friends, say そうだね (sou da ne) or the softer そうね (sou ne). You can also just say うん、そうだね (Yeah, that's right).

intro: えっ (eh) is a short "Huh?" or "What?" that Japanese speakers make when they are surprised or did not quite catch something. A long えー or えええ！ shows bigger shock or disappointment. It is one of the most recognizable sounds in anime.
literal: えっ is an interjection with no kanji. The small っ at the end shows the sound is cut off sharply.
usage: A quick えっ？ means "Huh?" or "Wait, what?" when you hear something surprising or did not hear clearly.
A long えー can show disappointment or reluctance, like "Aww" or "Ugh, really?" A loud, rising えええ！ is big shock.

A short えっ is natural in almost any situation, even with a boss, usually followed by something polite like えっ、そうなんですか. A drawn-out えー in response to a request from a superior sounds childish and like complaining.
Do not confuse it with ええ (ee) said calmly with falling tone. That is a slightly formal "yes."

forms.note: Disappointment, reluctance or doubt.
Surprise at news.
A different word, not surprise.

examples.context: Hearing that class is canceled today

A friend says the trip leaves at 5 a.m.

faq.q: What does eh mean in Japanese?
faq.a: えっ is a sound of surprise, like "Huh?" or "What?" A long えー can also mean "Aww" when someone is disappointed.

faq.q: What is the difference between eh and ee?
faq.a: えっ is short and surprised. ええ said calmly with a falling tone is a polite "yes." A long えー with strong emotion is surprise or disappointment, so tone tells them apart.

intro: あらあら (ara ara) means "Oh my" or "Oh dear." It is a gentle interjection used mostly by women, especially mothers and older women, when something mildly surprising or troublesome happens. In anime it is the signature phrase of calm, mature, sometimes teasing older female characters.
literal: あら is an interjection of mild surprise, used mainly by women. Repeating it as あらあら softens it and adds a tone of warm, amused concern.
usage: In real life you hear あらあら from older women, such as a grandmother watching a child spill juice: "Oh dear, oh dear." It sounds warm, not angry.
It can be sympathetic (あらあら、大変ね, "Oh dear, that must be hard") or gently amused, as if watching a child do something silly.
In anime, あらあら became a trope for a calm, mature woman, sometimes with a teasing or flirty edge. That flirty nuance mostly belongs to fiction. In daily life it sounds motherly or grandmotherly.
Men rarely say あら or あらあら, and from a man it sounds feminine or joking. Older men are more likely to say おやおや.

forms.note: The single form, mostly used by women.
Sounds like an older woman.
Similar feeling, more common from older men.

examples.en: Oh dear, did you spill it?

examples.en: Oh dear, that must be hard.

faq.q: Who says ara ara?
faq.a: Mostly women, especially mothers and older women. It sounds gentle and a little old-fashioned. Young people and men rarely say it except as a joke.

faq.q: Is ara ara flirty?
faq.a: In real life, no. It just means "Oh my" or "Oh dear." The flirty or teasing image comes from how some anime characters use it.

intro: やった (yatta) means "Yay!" or "I did it!" It is the past form of やる (to do), shouted when something good happens, like passing an exam or winning a game. It is a classic cheer in anime and in everyday life.
literal: やった is the past form of the verb やる, a casual word for "do." Literally it means "did," as in "(I) did it."
usage: Shout やった！ or stretch it to やったー！ when you succeed or get good news. It works for luck too, not just effort, like getting a day off or a free dessert.
やったね！ celebrates with someone else: "You did it!" or "We did it!" やったぜ is a rough, masculine version.
It is casual and emotional. When good news comes from your boss, say ありがとうございます or よかったです rather than shouting. A quiet やった to yourself is natural anywhere.
やった is also just the normal past of やる: 宿題やった？ means "Did you do your homework?" Context shows whether it is a cheer.

forms.note: Stretched for extra joy.

forms.en: You did it! / We did it!
forms.note: Celebrating with someone.
Rough and masculine.

faq.q: What does yatta mean?
faq.a: やった means "Yay!" or "I did it!" It is the past form of やる (to do) and is shouted when something good happens.

faq.q: What is the difference between yatta and yoshi?
faq.a: やった celebrates something good that already happened. よし is "All right!" and is often said before starting something, or when checking that something is done.

intro: よし (yoshi) is an exclamation meaning "All right!" or "OK!" People say it to psych themselves up before starting something, or when something is finished or checked. In anime, a determined よし！ or よっしゃ！ often comes right before a big effort.
literal: よし comes from the classical form of the adjective よい (good). As an exclamation it is roughly "Good!"
usage: Before starting something: よし、やるぞ！ means "All right, let's do this!" It is often said to yourself.
After finishing or checking: よし、できた (OK, done). Children are taught to say 右よし、左よし (right clear, left clear) before crossing a road, and workers use the same pattern in safety checks.
よしよし is what you say while patting a child or a pet: "There, there" or "Good boy/girl." よっしゃ is a rougher, more excited "Yes!", like a fist pump.
よし can sound like you are the one giving approval. A boss might say よし to an employee, but answering your boss's instructions with よし sounds wrong. Use はい or 分かりました instead.

forms.note: Rough and casual, like a fist pump.
While patting a child or pet.
Psyching yourself up.

examples.context: Sitting down to study
Finishing cleaning your room
A child checks for cars before crossing the street
examples.en: Right is clear, left is clear.

faq.q: What does yosh mean in anime?
faq.a: よし (often heard as "yosh") means "All right!" or "OK, let's go!" Characters say it to fire themselves up before doing something.

faq.q: Is yoshi also a name?
faq.a: Yes. Yoshi is also a common part of Japanese names, written with various kanji. As an exclamation, though, よし simply means "All right!" or "Good!"

intro: 痛い (itai) means "painful" or "it hurts." As an exclamation, 痛い！ or the short いたっ！ is "Ouch!" You hear it when someone stubs a toe, and in phrases like 頭が痛い (I have a headache).
literal: 痛い is an i-adjective. The kanji 痛 combines 疒, the radical used for illness, with a part that gives its sound.
usage: As "Ouch!": 痛い！ or the short いたっ！ Rough casual versions are いてっ and いてえ, mostly from men.
To describe pain, use [body part] + が痛い: 頭が痛い (headache), お腹が痛い (stomach ache). At a doctor's office you can point and say ここが痛いです (It hurts here).
It can also mean a painful loss or setback: その出費は痛い (That expense really hurts).
In slang, 痛い means "cringeworthy." 痛い人 is someone embarrassing who does not realize it. This is a mean thing to say about someone, so use it carefully.

forms.note: A quick reaction to sudden pain.
Use with a doctor or someone you don't know well.
Casual, mostly men.

faq.q: How do you say "it hurts" in Japanese?
faq.a: Say 痛い (itai), or 痛いです to be polite. To say where, use the body part + が痛い, for example お腹が痛いです (My stomach hurts).

faq.q: What does itai mean in slang?
faq.a: In slang, 痛い can mean "cringeworthy" or "embarrassing to watch." 痛い人 is someone who acts embarrassing without realizing it. It is an unkind thing to say.

intro: 怖い (kowai) means "scary" or "I'm scared." It describes something frightening, like a horror movie or a strict teacher, and also how you feel when you are afraid. You hear 怖い！ in anime and in real life whenever someone gets a fright.
literal: 怖 means fear or to be afraid, and い is the ending of an い-adjective. It is sometimes written 恐い, which has the same reading and meaning.
usage: 怖い is an adjective. In a full sentence it describes the thing that is scary: この映画は怖い means "This movie is scary." Said on its own, 怖い！ usually means "I'm scared!" Japanese often leaves out who feels the fear, so context tells you.

It also describes people. 怖い先生 is a strict, intimidating teacher, and 怖い人 is someone who seems scary or dangerous. Telling someone 怖い to their face is often a half-joking complaint between friends, but it can sound like a real criticism to someone you don't know well.

The past form 怖かった means "That was scary" or "I was scared," and people say it after a ride, a film or a near miss. In casual speech, 怖っ (kowa') is a quick reaction to something creepy or shocking, a bit like "Yikes."
To say that another person is afraid, Japanese uses 怖がる (to be scared of): 犬を怖がる means "is scared of dogs." Saying 彼は怖い means "He is scary," not "He is scared."

forms.en: That was scary / I was scared
forms.note: Past form, common after a scary experience.
Casual clipped reaction. Also written こわっ.
Used to describe someone else's fear.
Negative form.

Getting off a roller coaster
Warning a new classmate about a teacher

faq.q: How do you say "I'm scared" in Japanese?
faq.a: 怖い on its own already works as "I'm scared." Use 怖いです to be polite. To say what scares you, use が: 虫が怖い means "I'm scared of bugs."

faq.q: What is the difference between kowai and kowagaru?
faq.a: 怖い describes the scary thing or your own feeling. 怖がる describes someone else being scared, as in 子どもが雷を怖がる (The child is scared of thunder).

intro: さすが (sasuga) means "as expected" or "just what I'd expect from you." You say it when someone does something impressive that matches their reputation. In anime you often hear さすが followed by a name or title, and in real life さすがですね is a common compliment.
literal: さすが is an adverb meaning "just as one would expect." It can be written 流石, but those kanji are ateji (chosen for the word, not for their meaning), so most people simply write it in hiragana.
usage: さすが is praise that recognizes skill you already knew about. When a friend who is good with computers fixes yours in a minute, さすが！ means "I knew you could do it." The idea is that they lived up to what you thought of them.
You can attach it to a person or group: さすが先輩 ("As expected of you, senpai"), さすがプロ ("That's a pro for you"). The longer pattern さすが～だけある means "lives up to being ～."

さすがですね is a common compliment at work. Because it judges someone's ability, some careful speakers avoid saying it directly to a much higher superior in formal settings, but between coworkers and to teachers it is generally taken as friendly praise.
さすがに has a different feel. It means "understandably" or "even so, that's too much": さすがにそれは無理 means "That's really too much, no way." さすがの～も means "even the great ～": さすがの彼も疲れた (Even they got tired).

forms.note: A common compliment to coworkers or teachers.

faq.q: What is the difference between sasuga and sugoi?
faq.a: すごい is general amazement at anything. さすが praises someone for being as good as you already expected, so you only use it for a person or thing with a known reputation.

faq.q: What does sasuga ni mean?
faq.a: さすがに means "understandably" or "that's a bit too much." さすがに疲れた means "Understandably, I'm tired," and さすがにそれはない means "No, that's going too far."

intro: もう (mou) has two big uses. As a word in a sentence it means "already," "(not) anymore" or "more." As a reaction, もう！ is a frustrated "Geez!" or "Come on!" that you hear constantly in anime when someone is annoyed or embarrassed.
literal: もう is a native Japanese adverb, normally written in hiragana. Its core idea is going past a point: already done, no longer the same, or one more.
usage: "Already": もう食べた means "I already ate," and もう？ means "Already?" With a negative verb it means "not anymore": もう行かない means "I won't go anymore."
"More": with a number or amount it means "another" or "more," as in もう一回 (one more time) and もう少し (a little more).

As a reaction, もう！ or a drawn-out もう～ shows exasperation, often mixed with affection. もう、やめてよ means "Geez, stop it," and もう、しょうがないな means "Ugh, fine, I give up." Anime characters say it with a pout, and people really do say it, mostly with friends and family.
Be careful with もういい. It can mean "That's enough, thanks," but said in anger it means "Forget it!" and sounds cold. Don't use the pouting もう！ with a boss or customer.

forms.note: Also もう一度, which is a little more formal.
Can sound cold when said in anger.
もうすぐ着く: I'm almost there.
