faq.q: What does mou mean when anime characters say it angrily?
faq.a: It is a frustrated "Geez!" or "Come on!" Usually the speaker is annoyed or embarrassed but not truly angry, as in もう、バカ！ (Geez, you idiot!).

faq.q: What is the difference between mou and mada?
faq.a: もう means "already" and まだ means "still" or "not yet." もう食べた？ (Did you eat already?) is often answered まだ (Not yet).

faq.q: What does mou ii mean?
faq.a: もういい means "That's enough." Said calmly it can mean "I'm fine now, thanks," but in an argument it means "Forget it!"

intro: ダメ (dame) means "no good," "not allowed" or "don't." Parents say it to children, friends say it to stop each other, and anime characters cry ダメ！ to mean "No!" or "Don't!" It can also describe something hopeless or useless.
literal: It is written ダメ, だめ or 駄目. The word is commonly traced to the game of Go, where 駄目 is a point that belongs to neither player, so playing there gains nothing.
usage: Forbidding: ダメ！ alone means "No! Don't!" The pattern ～ちゃダメ (casual) or ～てはダメ means "You mustn't ～": 触っちゃダメ means "Don't touch."
Saying something doesn't work: 明日はダメ means "Tomorrow is no good for me." As a question, ダメ？ asks "Is that not OK?" and is often a gentle plea like "Pretty please?"
Describing things or people: ダメな人 is a hopeless person, and もうダメだ means "I'm done for" or "I can't go on." Calling someone ダメ is a put-down, but people often use it about themselves.
ダメです is direct. Staff talking to customers, or anyone turning down a superior, usually softens it to 難しいです (That's difficult) or ちょっと… instead of a plain "no."

forms.note: Casual. Polite version: ～てはいけません.

forms.en: I'm done for / I can't go on
forms.note: Said when exhausted or hopeless.

forms.en: worth a try, nothing to lose
forms.note: Short for ダメで元々.

examples.context: A parent stopping a small child
A friend suggests meeting tomorrow
examples.romaji: Ashita wa chotto dame nan da.
examples.en: Tomorrow doesn't really work for me.

examples.context: Near the end of a long run

faq.q: Is dame rude?
faq.a: Not by itself. It is a normal word for "no" or "not allowed." It is direct, though, so with customers or superiors people soften it. Calling a person ダメ is an insult.

faq.q: What is the difference between dame and iie?
faq.a: いいえ answers a yes-or-no question with "no." ダメ means something is not allowed or not OK. If someone asks "Can I come in?", ダメ means "No, you can't."

intro: うるさい (urusai) means "noisy" or "annoying." Shouted at a person, うるさい！ works like "Shut up!" or "Leave me alone!" Anime characters say it often, sometimes as the rougher うるせー (urusee).
literal: うるさい is an い-adjective. It is sometimes written 煩い, and also 五月蝿い, a playful spelling that literally means "flies in the fifth month." The basic idea is something that bothers you through noise or nagging.
usage: Describing noise is neutral: 隣がうるさい means "The neighbors are noisy." You can say it politely as うるさいです when talking about a place or a sound.

Saying it to someone is rude. うるさい！ to a person means "Shut up!" Between siblings or close friends it can be a normal grumble, but said to a teacher, boss, customer or stranger it is offensive and could start a real argument. うるせー and うっせー are even rougher and sound masculine.
It can also mean "fussy" or "picky": 味にうるさい means "picky about taste," and 口うるさい means "naggy." This use is not always negative.
In anime, embarrassed characters snap うるさい！ when teased. In real life, to ask someone to be quiet politely, say 静かにしてください or すみません、少し静かにしてもらえますか.

forms.note: Very blunt, masculine. Also うっせー.
A grumble, often to family.
A softer way to ask for quiet.
コーヒーにうるさい: picky about coffee.

examples.context: Construction noise late at night
examples.en: It's so noisy outside I can't sleep.

examples.context: A teenager to a parent who keeps reminding them
examples.en: Ugh, so annoying. I know already.

examples.context: Describing your father's taste
examples.en: My dad is picky about coffee.

faq.q: Is urusai rude?
faq.a: When you describe noise, no. When you say うるさい to a person, yes. It means "Shut up" and will offend anyone you are not close to.

faq.q: What does urusee mean?
faq.a: うるせー is a rough, slurred way of saying うるさい. It means "Shut up!" and sounds tough and masculine. Avoid it outside close friends.

faq.q: How do you politely ask someone to be quiet in Japanese?
faq.a: Say 静かにしてください (Please be quiet) or, more softly, すみません、少し静かにしてもらえますか (Excuse me, could you be a little quieter?).

intro: バカ (baka) means "idiot," "fool" or "stupid." It is the most common Japanese insult and one of the first words anime fans learn. How rude it is depends on your tone and who you say it to.
literal: It is also written 馬鹿, with the kanji for horse and deer. Those kanji were chosen for their sound. The true origin of the word is unclear, and the popular horse-and-deer story is only one of several theories.
usage: Said to a stranger, coworker, teacher or boss, バカ is a real insult and will offend. The verb バカにする means "to make fun of" or "to look down on" someone.

Between close friends, partners and family, a light バカ or バカだなあ can be teasing or even affectionate, like "you dummy." In anime, an embarrassed character yelling バカ！ often means "You idiot!" with a hint of "but I care."

There is a regional difference. In the Kanto area (Tokyo) バカ is the usual tease and アホ can sound harsher. In Kansai (Osaka) it is the other way around: アホ is the everyday tease and バカ can feel cold and hurtful.
バカ野郎 (bakayarou) is much stronger and angry, close to "you damn idiot." As a learner, avoid calling anyone バカ unless you are close and the tone is clearly joking.

forms.en: to make fun of, look down on
forms.note: 人をバカにしないで: Don't make fun of me.
Strong and angry. Often written バカヤロー.

forms.en: That's so stupid / I feel stupid
forms.note: Can be about a situation or yourself.
The everyday tease in western Japan.

examples.context: Teasing a friend who forgot their keys again
Telling off someone who is mocking you
Regretting a mistake

faq.q: Is baka a bad word?
faq.a: It is an insult, but a mild one compared to English swear words. With strangers or superiors it is rude and offensive. Between close friends it is often playful.

faq.q: What is the difference between baka and aho?
faq.a: Both mean "idiot." バカ is the common tease in Tokyo, while アホ is the common tease in Osaka and Kansai. Each can sound harsher in the other region.

faq.q: What does bakayarou mean?
faq.a: バカ野郎 means roughly "you damn idiot." It is much stronger than バカ and is said in anger, mostly by men in rough speech.

intro: やめて (yamete) means "Stop it" or "Please don't." It is the て-form of やめる (to stop, to quit) used as a request. You hear it in anime and daily life whenever someone wants another person to stop doing something.
literal: やめる means to stop or quit doing something, and its て-form やめて works as a casual request. In kanji it can be written 止めて or 辞めて (quit a job), but 止めて can also be read とめて, so やめて is usually written in hiragana.
usage: With friends and family, やめて or やめてよ asks someone to stop. The tone can be playful ("Stop, you're making me laugh") or completely serious.
やめてください is the polite version. It is still firm and direct, and it is what you would say to a stranger who is bothering you. Signs and staff use softer phrases such as ご遠慮ください (please refrain).
やめろ is the blunt command form, "Stop it!" It is rough and often heard from male characters in anime. In real life it sounds aggressive except in an emergency or a fight.
やめる also means "quit": タバコをやめて means "Quit smoking." Don't mix it up with とめて (止めて), which means stopping a moving thing, like asking a taxi driver ここで止めてください (Please stop here).

forms.note: Polite but firm.
Blunt command. Rough and aggressive.
Dictionary form.

examples.context: A friend keeps tickling you
Firmly telling a stranger to stop bothering you
Asking a partner to quit smoking
examples.en: I want you to quit smoking.

faq.q: What is the difference between yamete and yamero?
faq.a: やめて is a request ("Stop it, please"). やめろ is a blunt command ("Stop it!") and sounds rough and aggressive.

faq.q: Is yamete kudasai polite?
faq.a: Yes, it is grammatically polite, but it is still a direct demand. It is the right phrase when someone is bothering you, but it is too strong for gently asking a coworker to stop something.

intro: ちょっと待って (chotto matte) means "Wait a moment" or "Hold on." Friends say it when they need a second, and anime characters shout it to stop someone from leaving. It is casual, so add ください to make it polite.
literal: ちょっと means "a little" or "a bit," and 待って is the て-form of 待つ (to wait), used as a casual request. Together it means "wait a little."
usage: With friends and family, ちょっと待ってね is a soft "Just a sec," while ちょっと待って！ said quickly is an urgent "Wait!"
ちょっと待ってください is polite enough for most people. Shop staff and people on the phone use the more formal 少々お待ちください (Please wait a moment). With a boss or client, 少々お待ちいただけますか is safest.
It also works as an objection, like "Hold on, that's not right": ちょっと待って、それおかしくない？ (Wait, isn't that strange?).
In very casual speech people shorten it to 待って or even ちょ、待って. 待て is a blunt command ("Wait!") that sounds rough or bossy.

forms.ja: ちょっと待ってください
forms.note: Polite, fine with most people.
Used by staff and in business.
Blunt command. Rough.

examples.context: A friend starts walking off without you
Answering a friend calling from the door
Disagreeing in a meeting
examples.romaji: Chotto matte kudasai. Sore wa chigau to omoimasu.
examples.en: Wait a moment, please. I don't think that's right.

faq.q: How do you say "wait" politely in Japanese?
faq.a: ちょっと待ってください is polite for most situations. In business or as staff, say 少々お待ちください.

faq.q: What does chotto mean?
faq.a: ちょっと means "a little" or "a bit." On its own it is also used to soften a refusal: ちょっと… means "That's a bit difficult" without saying no directly.

intro: ありがとう (arigatou) means "thank you." It is the casual form, used with friends, family and people younger than you. To strangers or anyone above you, use the polite ありがとうございます.
literal: It comes from the adjective 有り難い (ありがたい), literally "hard to have," meaning rare and therefore precious. Its form ありがたく changed in sound to ありがとう. It is sometimes written 有難う, but hiragana is normal.
usage: Use ありがとう with friends, family, partners, children and people younger than you. With strangers, teachers, coworkers and anyone older, say ありがとうございます.
Friendly variations include ありがと (shortened), ありがとね (warm and casual) and どうもありがとう (a bit stronger). ほんとにありがとう means "Thanks so much, really."
Older customers sometimes say a casual ありがとう to shop staff, but as a learner the polite form is the safe choice with anyone you don't know.
In the Kansai area you may also hear おおきに, a regional way to say thanks.

forms.note: Common with friends and family.
A bit stronger than ありがとう.

forms.ja: ありがとうございます
forms.note: Use with strangers and superiors.

examples.context: A friend hands you a birthday present
A friend helped you move
Thanking a sibling who covered for you

faq.q: How do you reply to arigatou?
faq.a: Between friends, うん, いいよ or いえいえ are natural. どういたしまして (You're welcome) is correct but can sound a little stiff in casual chat.

faq.q: Is arigatou rude?
faq.a: No, but it is casual. Saying it to a boss, teacher or stranger can sound too familiar, so use ありがとうございます with them.

ja: ありがとうございます
kana: ありがとうございます
intro: ありがとうございます (arigatou gozaimasu) is the polite way to say "thank you." Use it with strangers, shop staff, teachers, coworkers and anyone older than you. It is the safe default for thanks in Japan.
literal: ありがとう comes from 有り難い ("rare, precious"), and ございます is a polite verb meaning "to be." The form ありがたくございます changed in sound to ありがとうございます.
usage: This is the standard polite thanks in shops, offices, schools and with anyone you don't know well. If you are unsure which "thank you" to use, use this one.
ありがとうございました is the past form. Use it when something is finished: after a lesson, when leaving a restaurant, or after someone has helped you. Staff say it to customers as they leave.
To make it stronger, say どうもありがとうございます or 本当にありがとうございます. 誠にありがとうございます is very formal and appears in speeches, announcements and business emails.
Between close friends it sounds distant or joking. In anime, polite characters, students talking to teachers and workers use it.

forms.ja: ありがとうございました
forms.note: Past form, for something completed.

forms.ja: どうもありがとうございます
forms.note: Stronger and still polite.

forms.ja: 誠にありがとうございます
forms.note: Very formal: speeches, business.
For friends and family.

examples.context: A clerk hands you your change
At the end of a lesson
Thanking a coworker who helped you
examples.romaji: Tasukete itadaite, hontou ni arigatou gozaimasu.
examples.en: Thank you so much for helping me.

faq.q: What is the difference between arigatou gozaimasu and arigatou gozaimashita?
faq.a: ございます is present and ございました is past. Use the past form for something that is finished, such as after a meal, a class or a favor. For something you just received, use the present form.

faq.q: How do you reply to arigatou gozaimasu?
faq.a: いえいえ (Not at all) is the most common. どういたしまして (You're welcome) is correct, and こちらこそ means "Thank you too."

intro: すみません (sumimasen) means "excuse me," "I'm sorry" and sometimes "thank you." It is one of the most useful words in Japanese. You use it to call a waiter, to apologize for bumping into someone, or to thank someone who went out of their way.
literal: It is the polite negative of 済む (すむ, to be settled or finished), so it literally means "it is not settled." It is often explained as the feeling that what you owe someone cannot be settled.
usage: Getting attention: すみません！ calls a waiter, a shop clerk or a stranger you want to ask for directions. It works like "Excuse me."
Apologizing: it is a polite apology for small things like bumping into someone or being a little late. For serious mistakes, especially at work, use 申し訳ありません.
Thanking: when someone picks up something you dropped or holds a door, すみません means "Sorry for the trouble, thank you." Many people say すみません、ありがとうございます together.
すいません is a common relaxed pronunciation, but in writing and formal situations use すみません. With close friends, ごめん is more natural.

forms.note: Past form, a fuller apology.
Formal apology for work and serious mistakes.
Relaxed spoken pronunciation.

examples.context: Calling a waiter at a restaurant
examples.en: Excuse me, we'd like to order.

examples.context: Arriving late to a meeting
Someone picks up the glove you dropped

faq.q: What is the difference between sumimasen and gomennasai?
faq.a: すみません is polite and works with anyone, including strangers and coworkers. ごめんなさい is more personal and is used with friends, family and people you know well.

faq.q: Can sumimasen mean thank you?
faq.a: Yes. When someone does something for you, すみません means "Sorry for troubling you," which works as a humble thank you.

intro: ごめん (gomen) means "sorry." It is the casual way to apologize to friends, family and partners. ごめんね adds a soft, caring tone.
literal: It comes from 御免, made of the honorific 御 and 免 (pardon, exemption). It originally referred to pardon or permission from someone above you. ごめんなさい adds なさい, so it literally asks for that pardon.
usage: Use ごめん with people you are close to. With a boss, teacher, customer or stranger, use すみません or 申し訳ありません instead.
ごめんね is softer and warmer. ごめんごめん is a quick, light "my bad," fine for small things but it can sound insincere if you really hurt someone.
It often comes before a refusal or a request: ごめん、今日行けない (Sorry, I can't make it today) or ごめん、ちょっといい？ (Sorry, got a second?).
ごめんください is a separate, polite phrase for calling out "Hello, is anyone there?" when you enter someone's home or a small shop.

forms.note: Warm apology to friends and family.
Light. Not for serious apologies.
Fuller and more sincere.
Said when entering a home or shop.

examples.context: Arriving late to meet a friend
Turning down a friend's invitation
examples.romaji: Gomen ne, kyou wa ikenai n da.

examples.context: Bumping into a friend's arm

faq.q: What is the difference between gomen and gomennasai?
faq.a: ごめん is short and casual, for friends and family. ごめんなさい is fuller and more sincere, and children use it with parents and teachers.

faq.q: How do you reply to gomen?
faq.a: いいよ (It's fine), 大丈夫だよ (It's OK) or 気にしないで (Don't worry about it) are natural replies.

intro: ごめんなさい (gomennasai) means "I'm sorry." It is fuller and more sincere than ごめん, but more personal than すみません. Children say it to parents and teachers, and adults use it with friends, family and people they know.
literal: It is ごめん (御免, "pardon") plus なさい, the command form of なさる (a respectful "do"). Literally it asks the other person to grant pardon.
usage: It is the word Japanese children learn for apologizing, so they use it with parents, teachers and other adults.

Adults use it for a sincere apology to a partner, friend or family member, and politely with neighbors or acquaintances. In business it can sound childish or too personal, so people say 申し訳ありません or すみません at work.
It also softens a refusal: ごめんなさい、その日はちょっと… (Sorry, that day is a bit difficult). It is the classic way to turn down someone who has confessed their feelings.
本当にごめんなさい (I'm really sorry) makes it stronger.

forms.note: Stronger, sincere.
Short form for friends and family.
Use at work and with customers.

examples.context: A child who broke a cup
You forgot a friend's birthday
Turning down someone who asked you out
examples.en: I'm sorry, I can't go out with you.

faq.q: Is gomennasai polite?
faq.a: It is polite enough for friends, family, neighbors and teachers. At work or with customers it can sound childish, so use すみません or 申し訳ありません there.

faq.q: What is the difference between gomennasai and sumimasen?
faq.a: ごめんなさい is a personal apology to someone you know. すみません is more neutral and also means "excuse me" and "thank you," so it works with strangers too.

intro: こんにちは (konnichiwa) means "hello" or "good afternoon." It is the standard daytime greeting in Japanese, used from late morning until the evening. You hear it when people meet neighbors, shop staff, teachers or anyone outside their close circle.
literal: こんにちは comes from 今日は (konnichi wa), "as for today," the start of longer greetings such as "How are you today?" The rest was dropped over time. That is why the last character is は, which is read "wa" here because it was originally the topic particle.
usage: Use こんにちは when you meet someone during the day: a neighbor in the hallway, a shop owner, a teacher, or someone you are visiting. It works for strangers and acquaintances and is polite enough for almost anyone.
Japanese people rarely say こんにちは to their own family or very close friends. Friends usually just say おはよう, よっ, or the other person's name. Saying こんにちは to a close friend can sound oddly distant.
Coworkers in the same company usually do not greet each other with こんにちは. They say おはようございます in the morning and お疲れ様です later in the day. こんにちは is used more with visitors and people from outside.
Before about 10 or 11 in the morning, use おはよう or おはようございます instead. Once it gets dark, switch to こんばんは.

forms.note: Use this instead of こんにちは in the morning.
Use this once it is dark.
A quick, relaxed spoken form. Not for formal situations.

examples.context: Meeting a neighbor outside on a sunny afternoon
Greeting a coworker from another company by name
A child greeting their teacher on the street

faq.q: Why is konnichiwa written with ha instead of wa?
faq.a: The last character is the particle は, which is always read "wa" when it marks a topic. こんにちは was originally 今日は ("as for today"), so it keeps that spelling. こんにちわ is a common casual misspelling.

faq.q: How do you reply to konnichiwa?
faq.a: Just say こんにちは back. With someone you know, you can add a little small talk, such as いい天気ですね (Nice weather, isn't it?).

faq.q: Can I say konnichiwa to my friends?
faq.a: You can, but it sounds a bit formal or distant between close friends. Friends usually use a casual おはよう, a simple "hey" like よっ or やあ, or just start talking.

intro: おはよう (ohayou) means "good morning." It is the casual form you say to family and friends, while おはようございます (ohayou gozaimasu) is the polite version for teachers, coworkers and strangers. It is one of the first words you hear in any school or home scene in anime.
literal: おはよう comes from お早く, from 早い (hayai, "early"), and is sometimes written お早う. おはようございます originally meant something like "It is early," a polite way to acknowledge someone up and about in the morning.
usage: Say おはよう to family members, friends and classmates when you see them for the first time in the morning. It is short, warm and very common.
Say おはようございます to teachers, your boss, coworkers, neighbors and anyone older or not close to you. In most workplaces, the polite form is the normal morning greeting.
It is usually used until around 10 or 11 in the morning. After that, people switch to こんにちは.

In some workplaces, such as TV, restaurants and part-time jobs, staff say おはようございます when they first arrive for a shift, even in the afternoon or at night. It works as "Hi, I'm here" rather than a comment on the time.

forms.note: For teachers, coworkers, bosses and strangers.
A shortened, relaxed form between friends and family.
Cheerful and cute. Only with close friends.

examples.context: Meeting a friend early at the station
Arriving at the office and greeting the boss
A parent greeting a child at breakfast

faq.q: What is the difference between ohayou and ohayou gozaimasu?
faq.a: おはよう is casual, for friends and family. おはようございます is polite, for teachers, coworkers, bosses and people you do not know well. If you are unsure, use the polite form.

faq.q: Until what time can you say ohayou?
faq.a: Usually until about 10 or 11 in the morning. After that, say こんにちは. The main exception is workplaces where staff say おはようございます at the start of any shift.

faq.q: How do you reply to ohayou?
faq.a: Say it back. Answer おはよう with おはよう, and おはようございます with おはようございます.

intro: こんばんは (konbanwa) means "good evening." It is the greeting for when you meet someone after dark. You hear it from TV and radio hosts, streamers starting a night show, and neighbors passing each other in the evening.
literal: こんばんは comes from 今晩は (konban wa), "as for this evening," the start of a longer greeting. 今晩 means "this evening" or "tonight." The final は is the topic particle, so it is read "wa."
usage: Use こんばんは when you meet someone in the evening or at night: a neighbor, a shop owner, guests at an event, or an audience. It is polite and safe with almost anyone.
Like こんにちは, it is rarely used inside a family or between very close friends. Friends meeting at night usually just say "hey" or start talking.
There is no fixed time to switch from こんにちは. Most people start saying こんばんは once it gets dark, so the time changes with the season.
こんばんは is a greeting for meeting, not for leaving. When you part at night, say おやすみなさい if the person is going to bed, or a normal goodbye such as じゃあね or 失礼します.

forms.note: The daytime greeting.
For parting at night or before bed, not for meeting.
Often seen in casual texts, but considered a misspelling.

examples.context: Visiting a neighbor's house in the evening
examples.en: Good evening. Sorry to bother you so late.

examples.context: A host starting a night radio show
Passing an acquaintance on a winter night

faq.q: Is it konbanwa or konbanha?
faq.a: It is pronounced konbanwa. It is written こんばんは with は because that character is read "wa" when it is the topic particle. Some romaji spellings write it as kombanwa, which is the same word.

faq.q: When do you switch from konnichiwa to konbanwa?
faq.a: When it gets dark. In summer that can be after 7 pm, and in winter it can be around 5 pm.

faq.q: Can you say konbanwa when leaving?
faq.a: No. こんばんは is only for meeting someone. When you leave at night, say おやすみなさい or a normal goodbye.

intro: おやすみ (oyasumi) means "good night." You say it to family, friends or a partner before going to bed or at the end of a late-night chat. The polite version is おやすみなさい (oyasuminasai).
literal: おやすみ is お plus 休み (yasumi, "rest"), from the verb 休む (yasumu, "to rest"). おやすみなさい adds なさい, a soft command, so it means roughly "please rest." The same word お休み also means "a day off" or "closed" (for a shop).
usage: Say おやすみ to people you are close to: family, friends, a partner, roommates. It is very common as the last message of the night in texts and chats.
Use おやすみなさい with parents in a polite household, teachers on a school trip, hosts when you stay at someone's home, and anyone older or not close to you.
You can also say おやすみなさい when parting from someone late at night if they are going home to sleep. It is not a general evening goodbye, though. Early in the evening, a normal goodbye fits better.
Watch for the other meaning. 明日はお休みです means "I have the day off tomorrow" or "We are closed tomorrow," and has nothing to do with sleeping.

forms.note: For anyone older or not close to you.
Stretched, relaxed version between friends.
Same word in kanji. Context shows which meaning is meant.

examples.context: Ending a phone call with a friend late at night
A child going to bed and saying good night to their parents
A last text to a partner before sleeping

faq.q: What is the difference between oyasumi and oyasuminasai?
faq.a: おやすみ is casual, for family, friends and partners. おやすみなさい is polite and works with anyone. Many families also use おやすみなさい with each other.

faq.q: How do you reply to oyasumi?
faq.a: Say おやすみ back, or おやすみなさい if they used the polite form. You can add また明日 (see you tomorrow).

faq.q: Does oyasumi also mean holiday?
faq.a: Yes. お休み also means a day off or a break, and on a shop sign it means "closed." For example, 明日はお休みです can mean "I'm off tomorrow."

intro: さようなら (sayonara, often spelled sayounara) means "goodbye." It is the word most English speakers know, but Japanese people use it less than you might expect, because it can sound final, like "farewell." You hear it most from school children to teachers, and in dramatic partings in anime and songs.
literal: さようなら comes from 左様なら (sayou nara), meaning "if that is so" or "well then." It was the start of longer parting phrases, and over time the first part alone came to mean "goodbye."
usage: At school, students say 先生、さようなら to teachers at the end of the day. This is one of the most common everyday uses.
Between friends, さようなら sounds stiff or overly final. People usually say じゃあね, またね, バイバイ or また明日 instead.
Because it suggests you may not meet again, さようなら fits long goodbyes: moving away, graduating, or ending a relationship. Saying it to a partner can sound like a breakup.
At work, people leaving the office do not say さようなら. They say お先に失礼します (Excuse me for leaving first), and others answer お疲れ様です.

forms.note: Shorter, slightly softer spoken form. Common in songs.
The normal casual goodbye between friends.
What you say when leaving work before others.

examples.context: Students leaving class at the end of the school day
Saying goodbye to a friend who is moving far away
A teacher ending the last class of the year

faq.q: Is sayonara rude?
faq.a: No, it is not rude. It can sound formal or final, as if you will not see the person again for a long time. For everyday goodbyes with friends, じゃあね or またね sound more natural.

faq.q: What do Japanese people say instead of sayonara?
faq.a: With friends: じゃあね, またね, バイバイ or また明日. At work: お先に失礼します or お疲れ様です. On the phone or in polite settings: 失礼します.

faq.q: Is it sayonara or sayounara?
faq.a: Both spellings refer to the same word, さようなら. The "ou" shows a long "o" sound. Sayonara is the common English spelling.

intro: またね (mata ne) means "see you" or "see you later." It is a casual goodbye between friends, family and classmates. You hear it all the time at the end of anime scenes, phone calls and chats.
literal: また means "again," and ね is a sentence ending that adds warmth and invites agreement. Together it is like saying "Again, OK?" meaning "Let's meet again."
usage: Use またね with friends, classmates, siblings and anyone you talk to casually. It often follows じゃあ (well then): じゃあ、またね.
You can make it specific: また明日ね (see you tomorrow), また来週ね (see you next week), またあとでね (see you later today).
It is too casual for a boss, a teacher or a customer. With them, say 失礼します, or a polite form like ではまた (until next time).
Unlike さようなら, またね suggests you expect to see the person again soon, so it sounds light and friendly.

forms.note: Equally common casual goodbye.
For people you will see the next day.
A bit more polite. Good in emails and with acquaintances.

examples.context: Waving goodbye to a friend at the station
Leaving a friend's house in the evening
examples.romaji: Mata ne. Ki o tsukete kaette ne.

examples.context: Ending a chat with a classmate

faq.q: Is mata ne polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Use it with friends and family. With a teacher, boss or customer, say 失礼します or ではまた instead.

faq.q: How do you reply to mata ne?
faq.a: Say またね back, or じゃあね. You can also add a wave and バイバイ.

faq.q: What is the difference between mata ne and sayonara?
faq.a: またね means you expect to see the person again soon. さようなら is more formal and can sound final, like a long goodbye.

intro: もしもし (moshi moshi) is how Japanese people say "hello" when they answer or start a phone call. It is also used to check if someone can hear you, like "Hello? Are you there?" You hear it in nearly every phone scene in anime and dramas.
literal: もしもし comes from 申し (moushi), a form of the humble verb 申す ("to say"). Repeating it, 申し申し, was a way to call out "I'm speaking" to get someone's attention. It was later shortened to もしもし.
usage: Use もしもし when you answer a phone call from a friend or family member, or when you call someone you know. It is often followed by your name: もしもし、田中です.
If the line goes quiet or breaks up, もしもし？ means "Hello? Can you hear me?"
In business calls, people usually do not start with もしもし. When answering at work, they say はい、〇〇でございます (Yes, this is [company]), and when calling a company they give their name and greet politely.
Some people also say もしもし to get the attention of a stranger, or jokingly to someone who is not listening. In everyday life, すみません is the normal way to get a stranger's attention.

forms.note: When the line is bad or the other person goes quiet.
A more polite way to answer, common at work.
Casual check during a call.

examples.context: Calling a friend and saying who it is
The call starts breaking up
Calling a friend who might be busy
examples.en: Hello, is now a good time?

faq.q: Do Japanese people say moshi moshi in business calls?
faq.a: Usually not at the start. When answering a work phone, people say はい、[company name]でございます. もしもし is mainly for personal calls, or to check the line during any call.

faq.q: Can you say moshi moshi in person?
faq.a: Rarely. Some people use it to get a stranger's attention or jokingly to someone who is not listening, but すみません is the normal way to get attention face to face.

intro: はじめまして (hajimemashite) means "nice to meet you." You say it the first time you meet someone, usually followed by your name and よろしくお願いします. It is the standard opening of any self-introduction in Japanese.
literal: はじめまして is also written 初めまして. It comes from 初めて (hajimete, "for the first time"), so it literally says something like "for the first time," meaning "This is our first meeting."
usage: Use はじめまして only when you meet someone for the first time. The usual pattern is はじめまして、[name]です。よろしくお願いします.
It is polite but not stiff, so it works with classmates, coworkers, a friend's parents and new people online. In very formal business settings, people may say はじめてお目にかかります instead.
Do not say it to someone you have already met. If you are not sure whether you met before, many people avoid it and just say こんにちは and their name.
On social media, people often open their first message to someone new with はじめまして.

forms.note: The same word written with kanji.

forms.ja: はじめまして、よろしくお願いします
forms.en: Nice to meet you, I look forward to knowing you
forms.note: The full standard introduction.

forms.ja: はじめてお目にかかります
forms.en: It is an honor to meet you
forms.note: Very formal. Used in business or with important people.

examples.context: Introducing yourself to a new classmate
examples.en: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka.

examples.context: Meeting a new coworker on the first day
examples.en: Nice to meet you. I look forward to working with you.

examples.context: A foreign student introducing themselves to a host family
examples.en: Nice to meet you. I'm from America.

faq.q: How do you respond to hajimemashite?
faq.a: Say はじめまして back with your own name. For example: はじめまして、佐藤です。よろしくお願いします. The other person may answer こちらこそ、よろしくお願いします (Likewise, nice to meet you).

faq.q: What is the difference between hajimemashite and yoroshiku?
faq.a: はじめまして means "This is our first meeting" and is said at the start. よろしくお願いします comes at the end of an introduction and means roughly "Please treat me kindly" or "I look forward to knowing you."

meaning: Please treat me well, nice to meet you
intro: よろしく (yoroshiku) is hard to translate, but it means roughly "please treat me well" or "I'm counting on you." People say it at the end of a self-introduction, when asking a favor, and when starting to work with someone. The polite full form is よろしくお願いします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu).
literal: よろしく is the adverb form of よろしい ("good, fine"), and is sometimes written 宜しく. So it means "well" or "favorably." よろしくお願いします literally asks "I request that things go well," meaning "Please be kind to me."
usage: After introducing yourself, end with よろしくお願いします. It means something like "Nice to meet you, and I hope we get along." This is expected in schools, workplaces and clubs.
When you ask someone to do something, add よろしくお願いします to mean "Thank you in advance" or "I'm counting on you." It is extremely common at the end of work emails.
Casual よろしく or よろしくね is used with friends and people your age. With anyone older, a teacher or a boss, use the full よろしくお願いします, or the more formal よろしくお願いいたします.
よろしく伝えて means "Say hi to [someone] for me." For example, お母さんによろしく means "Tell your mom I said hello."

forms.ja: よろしくお願いします
forms.note: The standard form for most situations.

forms.ja: よろしくお願いいたします
forms.note: Business emails and formal speeches.
The usual reply. Add お願いします to make it polite.

examples.context: Ending a self-introduction at a new job
examples.en: I look forward to working with you.

examples.context: Leaving the rest of a task to a friend
examples.en: OK, I'll leave the rest to you!

examples.context: Asking a friend to say hello to their mother
examples.en: Say hi to your mom for me.

faq.q: What does yoroshiku onegaishimasu actually mean?
faq.a: There is no exact English match. It means roughly "Please treat me well," "I look forward to working with you" or "Thanks in advance," depending on the situation. It is about asking for a good relationship or a favor.

faq.q: How do you reply to yoroshiku onegaishimasu?
faq.a: Say こちらこそ、よろしくお願いします, which means "Likewise." Between friends, こちらこそよろしく or just よろしく is fine.

faq.q: Is yoroshiku rude on its own?
faq.a: Not rude, but casual. With friends it is fine. With a teacher, boss or customer, use the full よろしくお願いします.

intro: 大丈夫 (daijoubu) means "OK" or "all right." You use it to ask if someone is OK (大丈夫？), to say you are fine (大丈夫です), and very often to politely say "no, thanks." It is one of the most common words in anime and everyday Japanese.
literal: 大丈夫 is written with 大 (big), 丈 (a length measure) and 夫 (man). It once described a strong, reliable man, and over time came to mean "safe" or "fine."
usage: As a question, 大丈夫？ (casual) or 大丈夫ですか (polite) asks "Are you OK?" after someone trips, looks tired or seems upset.
As an answer, 大丈夫です means "I'm fine" or "It's OK." It also works for "It's fine as it is" or "That works for me."
Be careful: when a shop clerk offers a bag and you say 大丈夫です, it means "No, thank you." Japanese people often use it to turn something down softly, so context tells you whether it means yes or no.
In casual speech you will hear 大丈夫だよ ("It's OK, don't worry") to reassure someone.

forms.note: Use with strangers, coworkers and anyone older.
Casual reassurance to friends and family.
A firmer, more formal way to decline.

examples.context: A friend trips on the stairs
Turning down a plastic bag at a convenience store
examples.en: I don't need a bag, thanks.

examples.context: Comforting someone who is worried

faq.q: Does daijoubu mean yes or no?
faq.a: Both, depending on context. 大丈夫です can mean "I'm fine" or "That works", but when someone offers you something, it usually means "No, thank you."

faq.q: How do you answer daijoubu desu ka?
faq.a: Say 大丈夫です (I'm fine) or はい、大丈夫です. If you are not OK, you can say ちょっと大丈夫じゃないです (I'm not really OK).

meaning: Yes; here you go; I'm listening
intro: はい (hai) means "yes." It is also used to answer roll call ("Here!"), to hand something over ("Here you go"), and to show you are listening. You hear it constantly in classrooms, shops, offices and anime.
literal: はい is a single word written in hiragana with no kanji. It is a reply word, like "yes" in English, and is more polite than casual うん.
usage: はい is the polite "yes." Use it with teachers, coworkers, customers and strangers. With friends and family, people more often say うん.
はい does not always mean "I agree." When someone is talking, はい often just means "I'm listening" or "I understand what you said." Do not assume it means the person accepts your idea.
With negative questions, はい confirms what the other person said. If someone asks 行かないんですか (You're not going?), はい、行きません means "Right, I'm not going." This is the opposite of English "yes."
はい also starts many everyday phrases: はい、どうぞ (Here you go), はい、わかりました (Yes, understood). Saying はいはい quickly can sound impatient, like "Yeah, yeah," so be careful with it.

forms.note: With friends and family.
A bit softer than はい. Common in conversation between adults.
Can sound dismissive or impatient.

examples.context: Confirming something a coworker asked
Handing someone a document
Accepting instructions from a boss

faq.q: Does hai always mean yes?
faq.a: No. Often it means "I'm listening" or "I hear you," not agreement. It also means "Here" at roll call and "Here you go" when handing something over.

faq.q: What is the difference between hai and un?
faq.a: Both mean yes. はい is polite and works with anyone. うん is casual, for friends and family.

faq.q: How do you answer a negative question with hai?
faq.a: はい agrees with the question as asked. To 寒くないですか (Aren't you cold?), はい means "Right, I'm not cold." If you are cold, say いいえ、寒いです.

intro: いいえ (iie) means "no." It is the textbook polite "no," but in real life it is used most often to brush off thanks or compliments, like "Oh no, not at all." Japanese people tend to avoid a flat いいえ when turning someone down.
literal: いいえ is written in hiragana with no kanji. It is a reply word meaning "no," the opposite of はい. The shorter いえ is also common.
usage: Use いいえ to say "no" to a factual question: Are you a student? いいえ、違います (No, I'm not). It is polite and fine with anyone.
A very common use is replying to thanks or praise: いいえ、どういたしまして (Not at all, you're welcome), or the quick いえいえ (Oh no, no).
When refusing an invitation or offer, a direct いいえ can sound cold. Japanese people usually soften it: ちょっと… (Well, that's a bit...), 大丈夫です (I'm OK, thanks), or すみません、今日は無理です (Sorry, I can't today).
With friends, people rarely say いいえ. They say ううん (nope) or いや (no, nah).

forms.note: Humble reply to thanks or praise.
With friends and family.
Casual. Also used to disagree or correct.

examples.context: Answering whether you are a student
Someone thanks you for holding the door
A coworker asks if you have eaten lunch yet

faq.q: Is iie rude?
faq.a: Not rude, but a flat いいえ to an invitation or request can feel cold. People usually soften refusals with ちょっと… or 大丈夫です. いいえ is perfectly fine for facts and for replying to thanks.

faq.q: How do you say no politely in Japanese?
faq.a: For facts, いいえ is fine. For offers, say 大丈夫です or 結構です (No, thank you). For invitations, say すみません、ちょっと… and let the sentence trail off.

faq.q: What is the difference between iie and iya?
faq.a: いいえ is polite. いや is casual and is used with friends, or to disagree and correct someone.

intro: お願いします (onegaishimasu) means "please" when you are asking for something. You use it to order food, tell a taxi driver where to go, ask a favor, or end a self-introduction with よろしくお願いします. The casual form is just お願い (onegai).
literal: お願いします is お (polite prefix) plus 願い (negai, "wish, request"), from the verb 願う ("to wish for"), plus します ("to do," polite). So it literally means "I make a request."
usage: Use お願いします to ask for a thing or a service. Point at a menu and say これ、お願いします (This one, please). Tell a taxi 駅までお願いします (To the station, please).
It also asks for favors and help, and is very common in fixed phrases: よろしくお願いします (Please treat me well) and もう一度お願いします (Once more, please).
お願いします and ください both translate as "please," but お願いします sounds softer and more polite. ください goes after a verb in て-form (待ってください, Please wait), while お願いします usually goes after a noun.
With friends, say お願い or お願い！ (Please, I'm begging you!). In very formal speech or business emails, use お願いいたします.

forms.note: With friends. Often with a pleading tone.
Business emails, formal requests, customer service.
Softer, more indirect request.

examples.context: Ordering at a restaurant while pointing at the menu
Telling a taxi driver where to go
Asking someone to repeat what they said

faq.q: What is the difference between onegaishimasu and kudasai?
faq.a: Both are used to ask for things. お願いします is softer and more polite and usually follows a noun (水をお願いします). ください often follows a verb in て-form (見てください, Please look) and can sound more direct.

faq.q: How do you reply to onegaishimasu?
faq.a: It depends on the request. A clerk will say かしこまりました (Certainly). Friends might say いいよ (Sure). After よろしくお願いします, reply こちらこそ、よろしくお願いします.

meaning: Please, go ahead, here you go
intro: どうぞ (douzo) means "please," "go ahead" or "here you go." You use it when you offer something, hand something over, or let someone go first. It is the offering side of "please," while お願いします is the asking side.
literal: どうぞ is an adverb usually written in hiragana. It is used on its own as a complete phrase, and also in front of requests to make them warmer, as in どうぞよろしく.
usage: Say どうぞ when you hand something to someone, often as はい、どうぞ (Here you go). It works with food, documents, tickets, gifts, anything.
Use it to invite someone to do something: どうぞ、入ってください (Please come in), どうぞ、座ってください (Please have a seat). The どうぞ alone, with a gesture, is often enough.
お先にどうぞ means "After you" when letting someone go through a door or take their turn first.
どうぞ is for offering, not for asking. To ask for something, use お願いします or ください. どうぞよろしくお願いします is a slightly warmer version of よろしくお願いします, common in introductions.

forms.note: Handing something over. Works with anyone.
Letting someone go first.
Eager, insistent offer. Friendly and a little humble.

examples.context: Handing a friend a drink
Holding the elevator door for someone
Inviting a guest to sit down

faq.q: What is the difference between douzo and onegaishimasu?
faq.a: どうぞ is for offering: "Here you go" or "Go ahead." お願いします is for asking: "Please give me" or "Please do this." A clerk hands you change with どうぞ, and you order with お願いします.

faq.q: How do you reply to douzo?
faq.a: Say ありがとうございます, or the shorter どうも. If someone lets you go first, すみません (sorry to make you wait) is also common.

faq.q: What does douzo yoroshiku mean?
faq.a: It is a warmer way to say よろしく at the end of an introduction, meaning "Nice to meet you, please treat me well." The polite full form is どうぞよろしくお願いします.

intro: ただいま (tadaima) means "I'm home" or "I'm back." You say it when you walk in the door of your home, and the people inside answer おかえり (welcome home). It is one of the first words you hear in any anime scene where a character comes home.
literal: ただいま is short for ただいま帰りました, "I have just now come home." On its own, ただいま (written 只今 or ただ今) means "just now" or "right now."
usage: Say ただいま as you step into your home, to whoever is there: parents, a partner, roommates, even a pet. Many people say it out loud even when nobody is home.
The normal reply is おかえり or the more polite おかえりなさい. The pair works like a small ritual, and leaving it out can feel a little cold in a Japanese household.
At work, people returning to the office from an errand or a client visit often say ただいま戻りました (I'm back). Coworkers reply おかえりなさい or お疲れ様です.
You will also see ただいま with its older meaning "right now" in formal phrases, such as ただいま準備中 (being prepared right now) on shop signs, or ただいま参ります (I'm coming right away) from staff.

forms.note: Used at work when returning to the office.
The usual reply to ただいま.
A shop sign meaning not open yet. Here ただいま means "right now."

examples.context: Coming home from school
Walking in the door after a long day
Returning to the office after a meeting outside

faq.q: How do you reply to tadaima?
faq.a: Say おかえり (casual) or おかえりなさい (polite). Both mean "welcome home" or "welcome back."

faq.q: Can you say tadaima at work?
faq.a: Yes. When you come back to the office, ただいま戻りました is the usual polite version. In a relaxed office, plain ただいま is also fine.

faq.q: Do you say tadaima if nobody is home?
faq.a: Many people still do, out of habit. Nobody will answer, but it is a normal thing to say.

intro: おかえり (okaeri) means "welcome home" or "welcome back." It is the reply to ただいま (I'm home), said by the person who is already inside. The polite form is おかえりなさい.
literal: おかえり is お (a polite prefix) plus 帰り (return), from the verb 帰る (to go home). It is often written お帰り. The full form おかえりなさい adds なさい, the command form of なさる, but in practice the phrase just means "welcome home."
usage: Family members, partners and roommates say おかえり when someone comes home. It is the natural answer to ただいま, and the two are almost always said together.
おかえりなさい is softer and more polite. Parents often use the short おかえり, while a host family, a younger family member or anyone being a little formal may use おかえりなさい.
It also works for "welcome back" after a trip, a hospital stay or a long time away, such as a friend returning from studying abroad. Coworkers say おかえりなさい when someone comes back to the office.
In maid cafes, staff greet customers with おかえりなさいませ, an extra polite form, as if the customer is coming home. In normal life you would not use that form.

forms.note: Softer and more polite than おかえり.
Mostly heard at maid cafes and in very formal service.
What the person coming home says first.

examples.context: A parent greeting their child after school
A host family member greeting a student
Meeting a friend back from a trip
examples.en: Welcome back! Was your trip fun?

faq.q: What is the difference between okaeri and okaerinasai?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. おかえり is casual and short. おかえりなさい is softer and more polite, good with a host family or coworkers.

faq.q: Is okaeri only used at home?
faq.a: No. It also means "welcome back" when someone returns from a trip, from an errand at work, or after a long time away.

intro: いってきます (ittekimasu) means "I'm off" or "See you later," said when you leave home and plan to come back. The person staying behind answers いってらっしゃい (see you, take care). You hear it every morning in anime as characters leave for school.
literal: いってきます is いって, the te-form of 行く (to go), plus きます, the polite form of 来る (to come). Together it means "I will go and come back." It is often written 行ってきます.
usage: Say いってきます when you leave the house for school, work or an errand, to family, roommates or a partner. It carries the idea that you will be back.
The reply is いってらっしゃい. When you come home later, the pair becomes ただいま and おかえり.
It is also used at work when stepping out for a while, like a client visit or lunch. In very polite business speech, people say 行ってまいります instead.
Do not use it when leaving a place you will not return to, such as a friend's house or a shop. There you would say お邪魔しました, じゃあね or 失礼します.

forms.note: The reply from the person staying behind.
Plain form, common with friends and family.
Formal version used at work.

examples.context: Leaving for school in the morning
Leaving home for the day
examples.romaji: Ittekimasu. Yuugata ni wa kaeru ne.
examples.en: I'm off. I'll be home by this evening.

examples.context: Stepping out of the office on an errand
examples.en: I'm just popping out to the post office.

faq.q: How do you reply to ittekimasu?
faq.a: Say いってらっしゃい. It means roughly "go and come back safely." You can add 気をつけてね (take care).

faq.q: Can I say ittekimasu when leaving a friend's house?
faq.a: No. いってきます means you are leaving and will come back. When leaving someone else's home, say お邪魔しました (sorry to have bothered you) or a casual じゃあね.

intro: お疲れ様 (otsukaresama) means "thanks for your hard work" or "good work." It is the standard greeting between coworkers in Japan, and also what friends say after a game, a practice or a long day. Most often you hear it as お疲れ様です or お疲れ様でした.
literal: お疲れ様 is お (a polite prefix), 疲れ (tiredness, from 疲れる, to get tired) and 様 (an honorific). It politely recognizes that the other person has worn themselves out working.
usage: At work, お疲れ様です is used almost like "hello" between coworkers: in the hallway, at the start of a phone call, and at the top of emails and chat messages. It is fine to say to bosses as well as to peers.
お疲れ様でした (past tense) is used when work is finished, for the day or for a project. When someone leaves the office saying お先に失礼します (excuse me for leaving first), the usual reply is お疲れ様でした.
Among friends, classmates and teammates, the short お疲れ！ is common after club practice, a test or a shift at a part-time job.

Avoid ご苦労様 toward people above you. It also means "thanks for your trouble," but it is said from a higher position to a lower one, so to a boss it can sound rude. お疲れ様 is the safe choice. It is also not something you say to customers.

forms.note: Said when work is done or someone leaves.

faq.q: How do you reply to otsukaresama desu?
faq.a: Just say it back: お疲れ様です. At the end of the day, reply お疲れ様でした.

faq.q: What is the difference between otsukaresama and gokurousama?
faq.a: Both thank someone for their effort, but ご苦労様 is said by someone higher to someone lower, like a boss to staff. お疲れ様 works in every direction, so it is the safe one to use.

faq.q: Can you say otsukare to friends?
faq.a: Yes. お疲れ is the casual form and is very common among friends, classmates and teammates.

intro: 頑張って (ganbatte) means "do your best" or "good luck." Japanese people say it to encourage someone before an exam, a match, a new job or any challenge. In anime you often hear the shouted form 頑張れ (ganbare) from the sidelines.
literal: 頑張って is the te-form of the verb 頑張る (to keep at it, to try hard), used as a request: "keep at it." The kanji 頑 means stubborn and 張る means to stretch or hold firm.
usage: Use 頑張って or 頑張ってね with friends, family and people younger than you before something hard: a test, a job interview, a performance, a race.

頑張ってください is the polite version. With a boss or someone much older, some people feel that telling them to try hard sounds a little like talking down. 応援しています (I'm rooting for you) is a safe alternative.
The usual answer is 頑張ります (I'll do my best) or, casually, 頑張る！ or ありがとう、頑張る.

Be careful with someone who is already exhausted, grieving or depressed. 頑張って can feel like pressure to push harder, and many Japanese people avoid it in those moments. 無理しないでね (don't overdo it) is kinder there.

forms.note: Shouted at sports and in anime. Casual and strong.
With strangers and people you are polite with.
The usual reply to 頑張って.
When you are in it together.

examples.context: Saying goodbye to a coworker starting a new job
examples.en: Good luck with your new job.

faq.q: How do you reply to ganbatte?
faq.a: Say 頑張ります (I'll do my best) or, with friends, うん、頑張る！ Adding ありがとう first is also natural.

faq.q: Is it rude to say ganbatte to your boss?
faq.a: Not rude, but some people feel it sounds like talking down. 頑張ってください is OK in many offices, and 応援しています (I'm rooting for you) is a safe option.

faq.q: What is the difference between ganbatte and ganbare?
faq.a: 頑張って is a gentle request, like "do your best." 頑張れ is the blunt command form, like "Go for it!" It is shouted at sports and used with close friends.

intro: 気をつけて (ki wo tsukete, pronounced "ki o tsukete") means "take care" or "be careful." People say it when someone is leaving, and shout it as "watch out!" when there is danger. It is one of the most common ways to send someone off in Japanese.
literal: 気 means mind or attention, を is the object marker, and つけて is the te-form of つける (to attach, to put on). Together it is roughly "put your attention on it."
usage: When a friend or family member leaves, 気をつけてね or 気をつけて帰ってね (get home safe) is a warm way to say goodbye, especially at night or before a trip.
As a warning, 気をつけて！ means "Watch out!" or "Careful!" To say what to watch out for, use に: 車に気をつけて (watch out for cars).
With strangers, customers or superiors, say 気をつけてください or the more polite お気をつけて. Staff often say お気をつけてお帰りください (please get home safely) to guests.
In letters and messages, 体に気をつけて (take care of your health) is a common closing line.

forms.note: With strangers and people above you.
Common from staff to customers.
Casual goodbye to friends.
Common at the end of letters and messages.

faq.q: Is it ki wo tsukete or ki o tsukete?
faq.a: Both spellings mean the same thing. The particle is written を, which is often romanized as "wo," but it is pronounced "o."

faq.q: How do you reply to ki wo tsukete?
faq.a: Say ありがとう (thanks) or うん、ありがとう. In a polite setting, ありがとうございます is fine.

intro: しょうがない (shouganai) means "it can't be helped" or "oh well." Japanese people say it to accept something they cannot change, like a cancelled train or bad weather. In anime it is also a fond sigh, like "you're hopeless, fine, I'll do it."
literal: しょうがない comes from 仕様がない (shiyou ga nai): 仕様 (a way of doing something), が (subject marker) and ない (there is not). So it means "there is no way to do anything about it."
usage: Use it when something goes wrong and nobody can fix it: rain on the day of a picnic, a sold-out ticket, a delayed train. しょうがないね shares the feeling with the other person.
しょうがないなあ said with a sigh is often affectionate. It means "Oh, fine" when you give in to a friend, a child or a partner, for example when you agree to lend them money again.
After a verb in the te-form plus も, it means "there's no point": 言ってもしょうがない (there's no point saying it).
It is casual. In polite or formal speech, 仕方がない or 仕方ありません is more common. Be careful saying it about someone else's serious problem, because it can sound like you don't care.

forms.note: Same meaning, a bit more formal.
Often affectionate, with a sigh.
For example 悩んでもしょうがない.

faq.q: What is the difference between shouganai and shikata ga nai?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. しょうがない is more casual and common in speech. 仕方がない sounds a little more formal and is used more in writing.

faq.q: Is shouganai negative?
faq.a: It is about accepting something you don't like, so it often sounds resigned. But しょうがないなあ can also be warm, when you give in to someone you care about.

intro: えっと (etto) means "um" or "let me see." It is a filler word Japanese speakers use while they think of what to say next. In anime, nervous or shy characters say it all the time.
literal: えっと is a shorter form of ええと, a hesitation sound. It has no kanji and no meaning of its own beyond showing that you are thinking.
usage: Use えっと when you need a second to remember something or find the right words: a name, a date, the answer to a question.
It is fine in everyday polite conversation, with shop staff or coworkers. In a formal speech or job interview, too many えっと can make you sound unprepared, so people try to keep it to a minimum.
Compared with あの, which softly gets someone's attention or opens a hesitant request, えっと focuses on you thinking. Many people say both together: あの、えっと…
Learners can use it too. It sounds much more natural in Japanese than an English "um."

forms.note: The fuller form, a little calmer.
Drawn out, when thinking longer.
Friendly, often when explaining something.

Trying to remember the way

faq.q: What is the difference between etto and ano?
faq.a: えっと means you are thinking. あの is used to get someone's attention or to start something you feel hesitant to say. あの can also mean "that" as in あの人 (that person).

faq.q: Is it unprofessional to say etto?
faq.a: Not in normal conversation. In a formal presentation or interview, try not to say it too often.

intro: あの (ano) has two uses. As a filler it means "um" or "excuse me," a soft way to get someone's attention or start a hesitant request. As a regular word it means "that," as in あの人 (that person).
literal: あの is a demonstrative meaning "that," for something far from both the speaker and the listener. The same word is used as a hesitation filler, often stretched to あのう.
usage: Before asking a stranger something, あの、すみません (um, excuse me) is polite and natural. It softens the start, so you don't sound abrupt.
あのさ and あのね are casual ways to start telling a friend something, like "hey" or "you know what." あのね sounds soft and is common with children and close friends.
As "that," あの always comes before a noun: あの店 (that shop), あの時 (that time). It also points to something both people already know about: あの話 (that thing we talked about).
In anime, a shy character saying あ、あの… shows nervousness. Real people do this too, but it sounds very timid if overused.

forms.note: Longer, more polite and hesitant.
To start telling a friend something.
Soft and friendly, common with children.

faq.q: What is the difference between ano and etto?
faq.a: あの is used to get someone's attention or open a hesitant request. えっと shows that you are thinking about what to say. People often use them together.

faq.q: What does ano ne mean?
faq.a: あのね means "you know what" or "listen." It is a soft, casual way to start telling someone something, and you hear it a lot with children.

faq.q: Is ano rude?
faq.a: No. あの、すみません is one of the most polite ways to start talking to a stranger.

intro: 好き (suki) means "like." You use it for things (猫が好き, I like cats) and for people. Said to someone directly, 好きです is the standard way to confess romantic feelings, the line you hear in countless anime confession scenes.
literal: 好き comes from the verb 好く (to like). The kanji 好 is made of 女 (woman) and 子 (child).
usage: Grammatically, 好き works like an adjective, and the thing you like takes が: ラーメンが好き (I like ramen). Before a noun it becomes 好きな: 好きな映画 (favorite movie).

Said to a person, 好きです or 好き does not mean a light "I like you as a friend." It usually means "I have feelings for you." This is the normal way Japanese people confess, and it carries more weight than the English "like."
To say you like a friend without sounding romantic, talk about what you like about them, or use phrases like 一緒にいて楽しい (I have fun with you).
The opposite is 嫌い (dislike). Saying 嫌い about a person is strong and can hurt, so people often soften it to あまり好きじゃない (I don't really like it).

forms.note: Also the standard confession line.
Before a noun: 好きな色 (favorite color).
Stronger and warmer than 好き.
The opposite. Strong when said about people.

faq.q: Does suki mean love?
faq.a: It means "like," but said to a person it usually means romantic feelings. Many Japanese couples say 好き far more often than 愛してる.

faq.q: What is the difference between suki, daisuki and aishiteru?
faq.a: 好き is "like." 大好き is "really like" or "love" and works for things, friends, family and partners. 愛してる is a deep "I love you" that is rarely said in daily life.

faq.q: How do you say I like you in Japanese?
faq.a: Say 好きです (polite) or 好き (casual). Adding だよ or なんだ, as in 好きなんだ, makes it sound more heartfelt.

intro: 大好き (daisuki) means "really like" or "love." You can say it about food, hobbies, pets, family, friends and partners. It is warmer and much more common than 愛してる, so it is often the closest everyday match for "I love you."
literal: 大好き is 大 (big, very) plus 好き (liked). So it means "very much liked."
usage: For things, 大好き is just a stronger 好き: 甘いものが大好き (I love sweets). The thing you love takes が.
Family members say 大好き to each other often, especially parents and young children. Between partners it is a common, sweet way to say "I love you" without the heavy feel of 愛してる.
Between friends, 大好き can sound cheerful and affectionate rather than romantic, especially in a group (みんな大好き！). Said one-on-one in a serious tone, it may be taken as a confession.
The opposite is 大嫌い (hate). It is very strong, but in anime and between couples it is sometimes said half jokingly when someone is pouting.

forms.note: Polite version, also used in confessions.
Warm and reassuring.
Only for food: ラーメンが大好物.
The strong opposite.

faq.q: Is daisuki romantic?
faq.a: It can be. Between partners it means "I love you." But families and friends also say it, and for things like food it just means "I love it."

faq.q: What is the difference between daisuki and aishiteru?
faq.a: 大好き is warm and everyday. 愛してる is deeper and much heavier, and many Japanese people rarely say it out loud. Most couples use 好き or 大好き instead.

intro: 愛してる (aishiteru) means "I love you." It expresses deep, serious love, and it is much heavier than 好き or 大好き. You hear it in songs, dramas and anime, but many Japanese people rarely say it in real life.
literal: 愛してる comes from the verb 愛する (to love), built from 愛 (love) and する (to do). 愛している means "am loving," and the casual form drops the い to become 愛してる.
usage: 愛してる is said between romantic partners or spouses, usually in serious moments: a proposal, an anniversary, a goodbye. It sounds intense, and in daily life it can even feel a little theatrical.
Many Japanese couples go years without saying it, and instead use 好き or 大好き. Not hearing 愛してる does not mean someone's feelings are weak.
Parents may feel deep 愛 for their children, but they usually say 大好き to them, not 愛してる.
Don't say it to friends, even as a joke, unless you know they will take it that way. In songs and anime it is far more common than in real conversation.

forms.note: More formal and serious.

Dictionary form, often in writing and lyrics.

faq.q: Do Japanese people say aishiteru?
faq.a: Rarely in daily life. It feels very heavy, so most couples say 好き or 大好き instead. 愛してる is more common in songs, dramas and anime.

faq.q: How do you reply to aishiteru?
faq.a: A natural reply is 私も愛してる (I love you too) or 僕も, depending on how you refer to yourself. A softer option is 私も大好き.

faq.q: What is the difference between aishiteru and daisuki?
faq.a: 大好き is warm and everyday, and works for family and friends too. 愛してる is deep romantic love, saved for serious moments.

intro: 恋 (koi) means romantic love, the feeling of falling for someone. It shows up in words like 初恋 (first love) and 恋人 (partner), and constantly in song titles and anime. It is a noun, so you don't say it to someone like "I love you."
literal: 恋 means romantic love or longing for someone. Its traditional form is 戀. It has the same reading as 鯉 (koi, the carp fish) and 来い (come here!), but these are different words.
usage: 恋 is the excited, longing side of love: having a crush, falling for someone, often before the feelings are returned. 恋をする or 恋してる means "to be in love."
愛 (ai) is deeper and broader. It includes love for family and humanity, and a long, caring bond. People often describe 恋 as wanting the other person and 愛 as giving to them.
Most of the time 恋 appears inside other words: 初恋 (first love), 恋人 (boyfriend or girlfriend), 恋愛 (romance), and 恋バナ (chatting about love lives).
To tell someone your feelings, use 好きです, not 恋. 恋 is for talking about love, not for saying it to a person.

forms.note: はつこい. Your first crush or love.
こいびと. A romantic partner.

faq.q: What is the difference between koi and ai?
faq.a: 恋 is romantic love and longing, often the early, excited stage. 愛 is deeper, more lasting love, and also covers family and friends.

faq.q: Is koi the fish?
faq.a: The fish is a different word with the same sound, written 鯉. Romantic love is written 恋. Context makes it clear which one is meant.

faq.q: What does koi no yokan mean?
faq.a: 恋の予感 means "a feeling that love is coming," the sense that you are about to fall for someone.

intro: 愛 (ai) means "love." It is the deep, lasting kind of love: for a partner, for family, or for people in general. You see it in song lyrics, movie titles, tattoos and in the phrase 愛してる (aishiteru, "I love you").
literal: 愛 is a single kanji meaning love or affection. It is read あい on its own and in compounds such as 愛情 (aijou, affection) and 恋愛 (ren'ai, romance).
usage: 愛 is a noun, and it sounds serious and a little literary. In daily conversation, Japanese people rarely say the word 愛 by itself. It is much more common in songs, poems, films and speeches.

愛 and 恋 (koi) are both "love," but they feel different. 恋 is romantic longing, often new or one-sided. 愛 is deeper and steadier, and it covers love for family, pets, a hometown or humanity, not only romance.
The verb 愛する (ai suru, to love) gives 愛してる (aishiteru), "I love you." Many Japanese couples find 愛してる too heavy for everyday use and say 好き (suki) or 大好き (daisuki) instead.
愛 also appears in many ordinary words: 愛情 (affection), 恋愛 (romantic love), 愛犬 (one's beloved dog) and 愛用 (something you use often and like). Ai is also a common girl's name.

forms.note: From the verb 愛する. Sincere and heavy; said in serious moments.
Warm feeling toward someone, often family or a partner.
Used when talking about dating and love stories.

faq.q: What is the difference between ai and koi?
faq.a: 恋 (koi) is romantic love or a crush, often full of longing. 愛 (ai) is deeper, lasting love, and it also covers family and friends.

faq.q: Do Japanese people say aishiteru?
faq.a: Not often. 愛してる is real Japanese, but it feels very heavy. Most couples say 好き or 大好き day to day and save 愛してる for rare, serious moments.

faq.q: Is Ai a Japanese name?
faq.a: Yes. 愛 (Ai) is a common girl's name, and the kanji also appears in names like 愛子 (Aiko).

intro: 心 (kokoro) means "heart" in the emotional sense, and also "mind" or "spirit." It is where your feelings live, so you hear it constantly in songs, anime and phrases like 心から (kokoro kara, "from the bottom of my heart").
literal: 心 is a single kanji usually explained as a simple picture of a heart. It is read こころ on its own and しん in compounds such as 心配 (shinpai, worry) and 安心 (anshin, relief).
usage: 心 is not the body part. The organ that pumps blood is 心臓 (shinzou). 心 is your feelings, your mind and your character all at once.
Common phrases: 心から (sincerely), 心が痛い (my heart aches, I feel bad), 心が広い (generous, open-minded) and 心を込めて (with all my heart), often said about a handmade gift or a meal.
In everyday talk, 心 sounds a little emotional or poetic. People usually talk about feelings with 気持ち (kimochi). You hear 心 more in lyrics, letters, speeches and dramatic scenes.
The しん reading shows up in many daily words: 心配 (worry), 安心 (relief), 中心 (center) and 本心 (true feelings).

forms.note: Used in heartfelt thanks and apologies, like 心から感謝します.
A very common everyday word: 心配しないで (Don't worry).
Use this for the physical heart.

faq.q: Does kokoro mean heart?
faq.a: Yes, but only the emotional heart. 心 is your feelings and mind. For the physical organ, Japanese uses 心臓 (shinzou).

faq.q: What is the difference between kokoro and kimochi?
faq.a: 気持ち (kimochi) is how you feel right now, and it is the normal everyday word. 心 (kokoro) is your heart or inner self as a whole, and it sounds deeper and more poetic.

meaning: I want to see you, I miss you
intro: 会いたい (aitai) means "I want to see you," and in practice it is how Japanese says "I miss you." It fills love songs and dramas, and couples and close friends text it to each other all the time.
literal: 会いたい is the verb 会う (au, to meet) plus たい, the ending that means "want to." The kanji 会 means meeting or gathering, so the phrase is literally "want to meet."
usage: Japanese has no single everyday word for "I miss you." Instead people say 会いたい, "I want to see you." It is said to a partner, a close friend, or family who live far away.
Small endings change the feel. 会いたいな is soft and wistful. 会いたいよ is stronger, almost pleading. 早く会いたい means "I can't wait to see you." When people finally meet again, they say 会いたかった (I missed you).

会いたい is personal and warm. Said to someone you don't know well, it can sound too forward. In business, use the humble お会いしたいです (I would like to meet you) or お会いできるのを楽しみにしています (I look forward to meeting you).
Another way to say you miss someone is 寂しい (sabishii, lonely), as in いなくて寂しい (It's lonely without you).

forms.note: Past tense; said when you finally see someone again.

forms.en: I can't wait to see you
forms.note: Common in texts before a reunion or a date.

forms.en: I would like to meet you
forms.note: Humble and polite, for work or people you respect.

faq.q: How do you say I miss you in Japanese?
faq.a: The most natural way is 会いたい (aitai), "I want to see you." You can also say 寂しい (sabishii), "I'm lonely without you."

faq.q: How do you reply to aitai?
faq.a: Say 私も会いたい or 僕も会いたい (I miss you too). A short 私も or 僕も (me too) also works between close people.

faq.q: Is aitai always romantic?
faq.a: No. It is common between couples, but people also say it to close friends and family. With someone you barely know, it can sound too intimate.

intro: かわいい (kawaii) means "cute." Japanese people say it about babies, pets, clothes, food, characters and people they like. It is one of the most-used adjectives in Japan and has even become an English word.
literal: かわいい is sometimes written 可愛い, with 可 (can, possible) and 愛 (love), which fits the sense "lovable." Those kanji were chosen to match the word's sound and meaning, so most people simply write it in hiragana.
usage: People often say かわいい out loud as a reaction: seeing a puppy, a cute bag or a pretty dessert. It is often stretched out as かわいい〜！ for extra feeling.

Said to a person, かわいい is a compliment. To a woman or a child it is very natural. Said to an adult man, it means sweet or charming, and it is usually playful; some men would rather hear かっこいい (kakkoii, cool).
かわいい also means "dear" or "precious," as in かわいい孫 (a beloved grandchild). People even call older people or ugly-but-charming things かわいい.
Do not mix it up with かわいそう (kawaisou), which sounds similar but means "poor thing" or "pitiful."

forms.note: A safe compliment with anyone.
Casual, common among young people.
A different word. Easy to confuse.

Complimenting a coworker's new bag

faq.q: Is it rude to call a man kawaii?
faq.a: Not rude, but it may not be the compliment he wants. It suggests sweet or adorable rather than cool. Among friends it is usually taken as friendly teasing.

faq.q: What is the difference between kawaii and kirei?
faq.a: かわいい is cute, sweet or adorable. きれい (kirei) is beautiful in a more elegant, grown-up way. A puppy is かわいい; a sunset is きれい.

faq.q: How do you reply when someone says kawaii to you?
faq.a: A simple ありがとう (thank you) is fine. Japanese people often answer modestly with そんなことないよ (Oh, not really).

intro: かっこいい (kakkoii) means "cool" or "good-looking." People say it about a stylish person, a great play in a game, a sports car or a hero's big moment. It is the word you hear when someone does something impressive in anime.
literal: かっこいい comes from 格好 (kakkou, appearance, form) plus いい (good), so it literally means "good in appearance." In speech the long かっこう shortened to かっこ. It can be written 格好いい, but hiragana is more common.
usage: かっこいい works for anyone, but it is used most for men: a handsome actor, a stylish friend. Said about a woman, it means cool, confident or sharp rather than cute.
It also describes things and actions: a cool car, a sharp design, a brave decision, even a way of living (かっこいい生き方).
The opposite is かっこ悪い (kakkowarui) or ダサい (dasai, uncool, tacky). The verb かっこつける (kakko tsukeru) means to show off or try to look cool.
Polite: かっこいいですね. Young people, mostly guys, also say the slangy かっけー (kakkee).

forms.note: The direct opposite.
Often a gentle criticism: かっこつけないで (Stop trying to look cool).
Rough slang, mostly young men.

Talking about an actor with a friend

examples.context: Complimenting someone's new jacket

faq.q: Can you say kakkoii to a girl?
faq.a: Yes. It means she looks cool, stylish or confident. Many women like it, but if you mean pretty, かわいい or きれい fits better.

faq.q: What is the difference between kakkoii and kawaii?
faq.a: かっこいい is cool or handsome. かわいい is cute or sweet. A sports car is かっこいい; a kitten is かわいい.

intro: きれい (kirei) means "beautiful" or "pretty," and it also means "clean." People say it about a view, flowers, a person or a tidy room. It is more elegant and grown-up than かわいい (kawaii, cute).
literal: きれい can be written 綺麗, with 綺 (fine patterned silk) and 麗 (lovely, beautiful). The kanji are hard to write, so most people use hiragana.
usage: きれい is a な-adjective: きれいな花 (a beautiful flower), 空がきれい (the sky is beautiful). It ends in い but is not an い-adjective, so the negative is きれいじゃない, not きれくない.
About people, きれい means beautiful in an elegant, mature way. Calling an adult woman きれい is a strong compliment. かわいい is cute; きれい is beautiful.
The "clean" meaning is just as common: きれいな水 (clean water), 部屋をきれいにする (to clean up a room). It can also mean neat, as in きれいな字 (neat handwriting).
Polite speech uses きれいですね (It's beautiful, isn't it). It is a safe thing to say about scenery, food presentation or a garden.

forms.note: きれいな景色 (a beautiful view).
Common from parents to kids.

examples.en: The night view is so beautiful!

faq.q: Does kirei mean clean or beautiful?
faq.a: Both. Context tells you which. きれいな部屋 is a clean room, and きれいな人 is a beautiful person.

faq.q: What is the difference between kirei and kawaii?
faq.a: きれい is beautiful or elegant. かわいい is cute or sweet. A mountain view is きれい; a baby animal is かわいい.

faq.q: Is kirei an i-adjective?
faq.a: No. It is a な-adjective even though it ends in い. Say きれいな花, きれいだった and きれいじゃない.

intro: 気持ち (kimochi) means "feeling." It covers both emotions, like your feelings for someone, and physical sensations. The most famous phrase is 気持ちいい (kimochi ii, "that feels good"), said in a hot bath or a cool breeze.
literal: 気持ち combines 気 (spirit, mind, mood) and 持ち, a noun form of the verb 持つ (motsu, to hold or have).
usage: For emotions, 気持ち is the everyday word: 気持ちを伝える (to tell someone how you feel), 気持ちがわかる (I understand how you feel). It is more common in conversation than 心 (kokoro).

For the body, 気持ちいい means "feels good" or "pleasant," and 気持ち悪い (kimochi warui) means "gross" or "I feel sick." Said about a person, 気持ち悪い is a harsh insult ("creepy"), and the slang キモい (kimoi) is even ruder.
気持ちいい is a completely ordinary phrase in real life: people say it about a massage, a stretch, fresh air or a hot bath.
When giving a gift, Japanese people often say ほんの気持ちです, "It's just a small token of my feelings." It is a modest, polite phrase.

forms.note: Ordinary and common: baths, massages, nice weather.
About a person it means creepy, which is very hurtful.
Polite phrase when handing over a gift.

faq.q: What does kimochi ii mean?
faq.a: It means "It feels good" or "This is nice." Japanese people say it about a hot bath, a massage or a cool breeze. It is an everyday phrase.

faq.q: Is kimochi warui rude?
faq.a: About food or how you feel, no: it means "gross" or "I feel sick." About a person, yes. It means "creepy" and is very hurtful.

faq.q: What is the difference between kimochi and kokoro?
faq.a: 気持ち is the feeling you have right now, and it is the normal word in conversation. 心 (kokoro) is your heart or inner self, and it sounds deeper and more poetic.

intro: 夢 (yume) means "dream." Like in English, it covers both the dreams you have while sleeping and your hopes for the future. It is a favorite word in song lyrics, anime openings and graduation speeches.
literal: 夢 is a single kanji meaning dream. It is read ゆめ on its own and む in some compounds, such as 夢中 (muchuu, absorbed in something).
usage: For sleeping dreams, Japanese says 夢を見る (yume o miru), literally "to see a dream." 怖い夢 is a scary dream and 変な夢 is a weird dream.
For goals, people say 夢がある (I have a dream) and 夢を叶える (to make a dream come true). 夢は何ですか (What is your dream?) is a common question for children and in interviews.
When something wonderful happens, people say 夢みたい (yume mitai, "It's like a dream"). When something seems too good to be true, they ask 夢じゃないよね？ (This isn't a dream, right?).
夢中 (muchuu) means being absorbed in or crazy about something: ゲームに夢中 (hooked on games).

forms.note: Literally "see a dream." Not 夢をする.
Said when something great happens.
Uses the む reading of the kanji.

examples.romaji: Kinou, hen na yume o mita.
