faq.q: How do you say "I had a dream" in Japanese?
faq.a: Say 夢を見た (yume o mita). Japanese "sees" a dream with the verb 見る, instead of having one.

faq.q: What does yume mitai mean?
faq.a: 夢みたい means "It's like a dream." People say it when something wonderful or unbelievable happens to them.

intro: ツンデレ (tsundere) describes someone who acts cold or prickly toward a person they like, then shows a sweet, affectionate side. It is a famous anime and manga character type, and Japanese people also use it jokingly about friends and pets.
literal: ツンデレ joins two sound words: ツンツン (tsuntsun), which describes being curt or aloof, and デレデレ (deredere), which describes being lovey-dovey or melting with affection.
usage: The classic tsundere character insults or ignores their crush, then blushes and helps them anyway. A typical line is 別にあなたのためじゃないんだからね (It's not like I did it for you or anything).
The word grew out of otaku culture and spread into everyday Japanese in the 2000s. Today people use it lightly: a cat that ignores you and then wants to cuddle is ツンデレ.
Calling a real person ツンデレ is teasing, not an insult. It is playful among friends. It is a fun label, not a serious description of personality.
Related types include ヤンデレ (yandere, love that turns obsessive and dangerous) and クーデレ (kuudere, calm and cool on the outside). The verb デレる (dereru) means to show your sweet side.

forms.note: The cold half of the word.
The sweet half of the word.
Casual verb: 急にデレた (They suddenly got all sweet).

examples.context: Talking about your cat
examples.romaji: Uchi no neko, tsundere nan da yo ne.
examples.en: Our cat is kind of a tsundere.

examples.context: Teasing a grumpy friend who just said something nice
Chatting about favorite character types

faq.q: Is calling someone tsundere an insult?
faq.a: No. It is light teasing that means they act tough but are secretly sweet. Most people laugh it off, though it is best kept to friends.

faq.q: What is the difference between tsundere and yandere?
faq.a: A tsundere hides their affection behind coldness. A yandere shows too much love, to the point of being obsessive or dangerous.

meaning: love that turns obsessive or violent
intro: ヤンデレ (yandere) is an anime and manga character type: someone whose love becomes so obsessive that it turns unstable or even violent. The sweet, devoted side is real, but they may threaten or hurt anyone who gets in the way.
literal: ヤンデレ joins 病んでる (yanderu, sick or mentally unwell, from the verb 病む) and デレデレ (deredere, lovey-dovey). So it means affectionate to an unhealthy degree.
usage: A classic yandere seems cheerful and devoted, then becomes jealous, clingy and threatening toward rivals. Stories play it for horror or dark comedy.

It is a fiction trope. In real life the behavior it describes is controlling and dangerous, not romantic. People use ヤンデレ as a joke for a friend who texts too much, but calling a real partner ヤンデレ suggests something worrying.
Do not confuse it with ツンデレ (tsundere). A tsundere hides their affection behind coldness; a yandere shows far too much of it in a frightening way.
The word 病んでる is also everyday slang among young people for "I'm mentally drained" or "I'm in a dark mood," as in 最近ちょっと病んでる.

forms.note: Casual slang for feeling low or drained.
A different, much gentler character type.
Used to label characters or stories.

examples.en: Yandere are way scarier than tsundere.

faq.q: Is yandere the same as tsundere?
faq.a: No. A tsundere acts cold but is secretly sweet. A yandere is openly sweet but obsessive, and may become violent out of jealousy.

faq.q: What does yanderu mean?
faq.a: 病んでる (yanderu) means "sick" in a mental or emotional sense. Young people use it casually to say they feel low or drained.

intro: オタク (otaku) means a devoted fan or geek: someone deeply into anime, manga, games, idols, trains or any hobby. In English it usually means an anime fan, but in Japanese it can be about almost anything.
literal: お宅 (otaku) is a polite word for "your home" and can also mean "you." The fan meaning spread in the 1980s and is usually explained as coming from fans who addressed each other as おたく. In the fan sense it is written in katakana or hiragana.
usage: The word once had a negative image: socially awkward, stuck indoors. Since the 2000s it has become much more neutral, and many Japanese people call themselves オタク proudly or as a joke.
It attaches to any hobby: アニメオタク (anime fan), 鉄道オタク (train fan), ゲームオタク (game fan). The short form オタ appears in words like アニオタ, ドルオタ (idol fan) and オタ活 (fan activities).
Calling someone else オタク can still sound like a put-down, depending on tone, especially if they don't see themselves that way. Using it about yourself is always safe.
The original お宅 is still used in polite speech for someone's home, as in 田中さんのお宅 (the Tanaka home).

forms.note: Short for アニメオタク.
Going to events, buying merch, supporting a favorite.
The original meaning, written in kanji.

Talking about your brother's hobby

examples.context: Sharing weekend plans
examples.romaji: Shuumatsu wa otaku nakama to ibento ni iku.

faq.q: Is otaku an insult?
faq.a: It can be, depending on tone. Calling yourself オタク is normal and often proud. Calling someone else otaku can sound like a put-down if they don't use the word for themselves.

faq.q: What is the difference between otaku and weeb?
faq.a: "Weeb" is English internet slang for a non-Japanese person obsessed with Japanese culture. オタク is a Japanese word for a devoted fan of any hobby, not only anime.

intro: 神 (kami) means "god" or "spirit." In Shinto, kami are the gods and spirits found in nature, places and ancestors. In modern slang, 神 also means "amazing" or "godlike," so fans call a great player or a brilliant game 神.
literal: 神 is a single kanji meaning god or spirit. It is read かみ on its own and じん or しん in compounds such as 神社 (jinja, shrine) and 神道 (shintou, Shinto). 神様 (kamisama) adds the honorific 様.
usage: In Shinto there are countless kami, often described as 八百万の神 (yaoyorozu no kami, "eight million gods"). People say 神様 (kamisama) when talking to or about a god respectfully, as in 神様、お願い (Please, God).
神 can mean God in other religions too, depending on context. The word itself is neutral and fits whichever god the speaker means.

In slang, 神 means amazing: 神ゲー (kamigee, an amazing game), 神回 (kamikai, an amazing episode) and 神対応 (kami taiou, wonderfully kind treatment, often from a celebrity to fans). This is casual and very common online.
かみ has homophones: 紙 (paper) and 髪 (hair). Context almost always makes the meaning clear.

forms.note: How people usually say "God" when praying or speaking of a god.
Slang for a standout episode of a show.
Slang praise for great service or fan treatment.

examples.context: Making a wish at a shrine
Finishing a great video game
Talking about last night's episode
examples.romaji: Kinou no kai wa kamikai datta.

faq.q: What does kamisama mean?
faq.a: 神様 (kamisama) means "god" with the respectful ending 様. It is the normal way to say God when praying or speaking about a god.

faq.q: What does kami mean in slang?
faq.a: It means amazing or godlike. Fans say 神 about a brilliant player, a great game or a perfect episode, as in 神ゲー or 神回.

faq.q: Does kami also mean paper and hair?
faq.a: They sound the same but are different words: 紙 (paper) and 髪 (hair). The kanji and context tell them apart.

intro: 鬼 (oni) is a demon or ogre from Japanese folklore: a big horned creature, often red or blue, carrying an iron club. The word also means "it" in tag, a harsh, strict person, and in slang, "super" or "extremely."
literal: 鬼 is a single kanji. In Chinese it refers to ghosts or spirits of the dead; in Japanese it came to mean the horned ogre of folk tales. It is read おに on its own and き in some compounds, such as 鬼門 (kimon, an unlucky direction).
usage: Oni appear in many folk tales and festivals. On 節分 (Setsubun, in early February), families throw roasted soybeans and shout 鬼は外、福は内 ("Demons out, good luck in"). Often a parent wears an oni mask.
In children's games, the person who is "it" is 鬼. Tag is 鬼ごっこ (onigokko), and in hide-and-seek the seeker is also 鬼.
鬼 describes harsh people: 鬼コーチ (a brutally strict coach), 鬼上司 (a demon boss). Calling someone 鬼！ to their face means "You're heartless!" It is usually half-joking, but it can sting.
In casual slang, 鬼 works as "super": 鬼かわいい (super cute), 鬼むず (super hard). 鬼のように means "like crazy": 鬼のように忙しい (insanely busy).

forms.note: The person who chases is the 鬼.
Shouted while throwing beans at Setsubun.
Common in sports talk.

faq.q: What is an oni?
faq.a: An oni is a horned ogre or demon from Japanese folklore, usually red or blue with a club. They are scary in old tales, but also appear in festivals and on cute goods.

faq.q: Is calling someone oni rude?
faq.a: It means they are harsh or heartless. Between friends it is usually a joke, like after a tough workout. Said seriously, it is a real criticism.

faq.q: What does oni mean in slang?
faq.a: Young people use 鬼 to mean "super" or "extremely," as in 鬼かわいい (super cute). It is casual slang.

intro: ちび (chibi) means "shorty" or "little one." In Japanese it is a casual word for a small person, a small child or a small pet. English-speaking fans also use "chibi" for the cute art style with big heads and tiny bodies.
literal: ちび is a native Japanese word, usually written in hiragana or katakana (チビ). It is often connected to the verb ちびる, which describes something worn down and short, like a stubby pencil.
usage: In everyday Japanese, ちび is said about someone who is small. Parents and relatives use it warmly for little kids, as in うちのちび ("my little one"), and people use it as a nickname for small pets.

Said to a teenager or adult, ちび is teasing about their height. Between close friends it can be playful, but many short people dislike it, so it can easily hurt. Do not use it with people you do not know well.
The English sense of "chibi" as an art style is less common in Japan. Japanese fans more often say デフォルメ (deformed style) or SDキャラ, although ちびキャラ is also understood.
In anime, a character who is short often shouts ちびって言うな ("Don't call me shorty!"). This is a joke about how sensitive the word can be.

forms.note: A friendly word for young children, common in ads and events.
Affectionate, said to small children or pets.
Small, cute versions of characters, also called SDキャラ.

faq.q: Is chibi an insult?
faq.a: It can be. For small kids and pets it is warm and cute. Said to a teen or adult, it teases them about being short, and many people find that annoying or hurtful.

faq.q: What do Japanese people call the chibi art style?
faq.a: Most often デフォルメ (deformed style) or SDキャラ (super-deformed character). ちびキャラ is also used and understood.

meaning: strong affection for a cute character
intro: 萌え (moe) is fan slang for the warm, protective affection you feel toward a cute character. People say a character or a trait is 萌え, or that it makes them 萌える. It comes from otaku culture and is now known well beyond it.
literal: 萌え comes from the verb 萌える, which means "to sprout" or "to bud," as plants do in spring. How it became slang is not certain. A common explanation is that it started as a play on 燃える (to burn), which sounds the same.
usage: 萌え describes a feeling more than a quality. If a character's shy smile makes you want to protect them, that feeling is 萌え. Fans say things like このキャラ萌える ("This character gets me").
It also attaches to traits: メガネ萌え means being drawn to characters with glasses, and ギャップ萌え is the charm of a gap, such as a tough character who loves kittens.
The word peaked in the 2000s and now sounds a little dated. Younger fans more often say 尊い (precious), 推し (favorite) or かわいい. Outside fan circles, people may connect 萌え with otaku stereotypes.
The maid cafe chant 萌え萌えキュン is a performance, not something people say in normal conversation.

forms.note: The verb form, as in めっちゃ萌える.
Charm from an unexpected contrast in someone's personality.
A character designed to be cute, including mascots.
Long sleeves that cover the hands, seen as cute.

faq.q: What does moe mean in anime?
faq.a: It is the feeling of warm, protective affection toward a cute character, or the traits that cause that feeling. A character can be called 萌え, and fans say it makes them 萌える.

faq.q: Is moe still used in Japan?
faq.a: Yes, but it sounds a bit dated. Many fans now prefer words like 尊い (precious) or 推し (favorite). Compounds like ギャップ萌え are still common.

meaning: Are you stupid? / Are you an idiot?
intro: バカじゃないの (baka ja nai no) means "Are you stupid?" or "Are you an idiot?" It is said when someone does or says something you find silly or unbelievable. In anime it is a classic line for a character who is embarrassed and covers it by acting annoyed.
literal: バカ means "fool," じゃない means "isn't," and の turns it into a question. Word for word it is "Aren't you a fool?" It is a rhetorical question, so no answer is expected.
usage: This is a casual and rude phrase. It mocks the other person's judgment. Between close friends it can be playful, but said to a coworker, a stranger or anyone older, it is insulting.
Tone changes everything. A laughing バカじゃないの？ to a friend who did something silly is teasing. A cold, flat バカじゃないの is a real put-down and can start an argument.

In anime, a character who is secretly pleased or embarrassed often says it to hide their feelings, a pattern tied to the tsundere type. In real life people say it less often, and usually only to people they are very close to.
Rougher versions are バカじゃね？ and バカなの？. Do not use any of them in polite situations.

forms.note: Shorter and just as blunt.
Rough slang, mostly young men.
The base word on its own.

faq.q: Is baka ja nai no rude?
faq.a: Yes. It questions the other person's intelligence. Close friends may say it as a joke, but with anyone else it is insulting.

faq.q: Why do tsundere characters say baka ja nai no?
faq.a: It lets them hide embarrassment or affection behind annoyance. The real meaning is often closer to "Stop it, you're making me blush."

intro: 行くぞ (iku zo) means "Let's go!" or "Here I come!" A leader shouts it to get a group moving, and a fighter says it right before attacking. It is a strong, energetic phrase heard constantly in anime, sports and games.
literal: 行く means "to go," and ぞ is a sentence ending that adds force, like an exclamation mark. Together it is "I'm going!" or "We're going!" with strong emphasis.
usage: When said to a group, 行くぞ means "Let's go!" or "Come on!" A coach, captain or older sibling might say 行くぞ to get everyone moving. Unlike 行こう, it sounds like a command from someone in charge.
Before an attack or a challenge, 行くぞ means "Here I come!" It warns the other person and builds tension, which is why it is so common in fight scenes.
ぞ sounds rough and masculine. Men use it with friends, family and teammates. Women more often say 行くよ, although some use 行くぞ for energy.
Do not say it to a boss, teacher or customer. Use 行きましょう ("Shall we go?") instead.

forms.note: Neutral and friendly, used by everyone.
Softer, common among women and with kids.
Even rougher and more macho than 行くぞ.
Polite; use with superiors.

examples.context: A team captain before a match
A father getting the family out the door
A fighter about to attack

faq.q: What is the difference between iku zo and ikou?
faq.a: 行こう is a friendly "Let's go" that anyone can say. 行くぞ is stronger and sounds like a leader giving a command or a fighter warning an opponent.

faq.q: Can girls say iku zo?
faq.a: Yes, but ぞ sounds masculine, so it stands out. Women more often say 行くよ or 行こう in daily life.

intro: 貴様 (kisama) is a very rude, hostile way to say "you." In anime, villains and angry warriors shout it at enemies, much like "you bastard" in English. In real life it is almost never used and would be deeply offensive.
literal: 貴様 is written with 貴 (noble, precious) and 様 (an honorific). It was once a respectful word for "you" in letters and formal speech. Over centuries its meaning reversed, and it became an insult.
usage: Calling someone 貴様 shows contempt and anger. It is stronger than お前 and close to てめえ. It is something you say right before a fight, not in a normal argument.

In real life you will almost never hear it. Using it with a friend, coworker or stranger would shock and offend them. Do not use it, even as a joke, unless the other person clearly knows you are quoting anime.
In anime and games it fits villains, samurai, soldiers and proud fighters. It often sounds old-fashioned or military, which is part of its dramatic effect.
The plural 貴様ら ("you lot") is just as hostile. If you need a neutral "you," use the person's name with さん, or あなた in writing.

forms.note: Plural, equally rude.
Rough street language, about as rude as 貴様.
Rude to strangers, but common among close male friends.

faq.q: How rude is kisama?
faq.a: Very rude. It shows open hostility, close to "you bastard." Using it in real life would seriously offend almost anyone.

faq.q: Why does kisama use honorific kanji?
faq.a: 貴 means noble and 様 is an honorific, because the word was once respectful. Its meaning shifted over time until it became an insult.

faq.q: What is the difference between kisama and omae?
faq.a: お前 is blunt and can be friendly between close male friends. 貴様 is almost always hostile and sounds more dramatic and old-fashioned.

intro: にゃ (nya) is the Japanese sound a cat makes, like "meow" in English. In anime, cat characters and playful characters also add にゃ to the end of their sentences to sound cute and cat-like.
literal: にゃ is an onomatopoeia that imitates a cat's cry. A longer meow is written にゃー or にゃあ, and にゃん is a cuter version.
usage: When talking about real cats, Japanese people say a cat goes にゃー or にゃあ. Children's books and parents use にゃんにゃん or にゃんこ for cats too.
In anime and games, cat-like characters end sentences with にゃ, as in そうだにゃ ("That's right, nya"). Some also swap な sounds for にゃ, so なに becomes にゃに.
In real life, adults sometimes use にゃ or にゃん in texts and on social media to sound cute or playful. Saying it out loud in normal conversation sounds like a joke or a performance.
February 22 is Cat Day in Japan because 2-2-2 can be read にゃんにゃんにゃん.

forms.note: The usual sound for a cat's meow.

A cute word for a cat.

faq.q: What sound does a cat make in Japanese?
faq.a: にゃー or にゃあ (nyaa). Cute versions are にゃん and にゃんにゃん.

faq.q: Do Japanese people really say nya?
faq.a: Not in normal speech. Adults sometimes use にゃ or にゃん in texts or jokes to sound cute, but saying it seriously sounds like an anime character.

meaning: what a pain, too much hassle
intro: 面倒くさい (mendokusai) means "what a pain" or "too much hassle." People say it when they do not feel like doing something, and lazy anime characters say it all the time. It is one of the most common complaints in casual Japanese.
literal: 面倒 (mendou) means "trouble" or "bother," and くさい is a suffix meaning "seeming" or "giving off a feeling of," from 臭い (smelly). The full reading is めんどうくさい, but in speech it is almost always shortened to めんどくさい.
usage: Use it about tasks: 宿題めんどくさい ("Homework is such a pain"). It expresses laziness or annoyance, not real difficulty.
Said about a person, あの人めんどくさい means they are difficult to deal with or high-maintenance. This is a negative judgment, so be careful who hears it.
It is casual. Saying it about a request from your boss or a teacher sounds lazy and rude. In polite settings people say ちょっと大変ですね ("That's a bit tough") instead.
Very casual speakers shorten it further to めんどい or めんどくせー. The second one sounds rough and is mostly used by young men.

forms.note: Even shorter slang.

faq.q: Is mendokusai rude?
faq.a: It is casual and sounds lazy. It is fine with friends, but saying it about a task from your boss or teacher is rude. Calling a person めんどくさい is a real criticism.

faq.q: What is the difference between mendokusai and mendoukusai?
faq.a: They are the same word. めんどうくさい is the full reading, and めんどくさい is the shorter form people actually say.

intro: いただきます (itadakimasu) is what Japanese people say right before they eat. It roughly means "I humbly receive" and works like a short thanks for the food. You hear it at every family meal in anime and in real life.
literal: いただきます is the polite form of いただく, a humble verb meaning "to receive" or "to eat and drink." It is often written 頂く, and 頂 means the top of the head. The usual explanation is that people once raised gifts from superiors above their heads.
usage: Say it just before your first bite, often with your hands pressed together. Everyone says it, at home, at school lunch, at restaurants and even when eating alone.
It expresses thanks to the people who made or paid for the meal and, in a broader sense, to the food itself. It is not quite "bon appetit," because the person eating says it, not the person serving.
If someone treats you to a meal, saying いただきます to them is a natural way to say thank you before you start.
It also works when you accept something offered, like a snack or a drink: じゃあ、いただきます ("Then I'll have some, thanks"). After the meal, you say ごちそうさまでした.

forms.note: Cheerful, stretched version common with kids and friends.

faq.q: Do you have to say itadakimasu in Japan?
faq.a: It is not a rule, but nearly everyone says it before eating. Visitors who say it make a good impression.

faq.q: How do you reply to itadakimasu?
faq.a: There is no set reply. Others at the table say いただきます too. The cook might say どうぞ (go ahead) or 召し上がれ (enjoy).

faq.q: What do you say after eating?
faq.a: ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita), which means "Thank you for the meal."

intro: ごちそうさま (gochisousama) means "Thank you for the meal." Japanese people say it when they finish eating, usually in the polite form ごちそうさまでした. It is the partner of いただきます, which is said before the meal.
literal: It is written ご馳走様. 馳走 (chisou) combines two kanji that both mean "to run," and once described running around to prepare food for a guest. ご and 様 add politeness, so the phrase thanks someone for that effort.
usage: Say ごちそうさまでした when you finish a meal at home, at a friend's place or at school. With family and friends, the shorter ごちそうさま is fine.
It is also common to say it to staff when leaving a restaurant, especially small places like ramen shops. The staff usually reply ありがとうございました.
When someone pays for your meal or drinks, say ごちそうさまです or ごちそうさまでした to them. This is an important courtesy toward bosses and older friends.
As a joke, people say ごちそうさま when a friend goes on and on about their partner. It means something like "Thanks, I've had my fill of that."

forms.note: The standard polite form.
Often said to someone who is paying.

faq.q: What is the difference between itadakimasu and gochisousama?
faq.a: いただきます is said before eating, and ごちそうさまでした is said after. Together they frame every meal.

faq.q: How do you reply to gochisousama deshita?
faq.a: At home, the cook often says お粗末さまでした (it was nothing special) or just はい. Restaurant staff usually say ありがとうございました.

intro: おいしい (oishii) means "delicious" or "tasty." It is the everyday word for food and drinks that taste good, and people say it out loud while eating all the time. In polite speech it becomes おいしいです.
literal: おいしい is often written 美味しい, using 美 (beautiful) and 味 (taste). Dictionaries trace it to the old word いしい (good, tasty) with the polite prefix お added.
usage: Japanese people often say おいしい! right after the first bite, even without being asked. Saying it to a host or cook is a natural compliment.
Use おいしいです with people you are polite to, and おいしかったです ("It was delicious") after the meal. おいしそう means "That looks delicious."
Men sometimes say うまい instead. It means the same thing but is more casual and a bit rough. おいしい works for everyone.
Saying おいしくない ("not tasty") to a cook is blunt. People soften it with ちょっと苦手かも ("I'm not really into this"). おいしい also has a slang sense of "profitable" or "a great deal," as in おいしい話.

faq.q: What is the difference between oishii and umai?
faq.a: Both mean delicious. おいしい is standard and polite enough for anyone. うまい is casual and sounds more masculine. うまい can also mean "skillful."

faq.q: How do you say it was delicious in Japanese?
faq.a: Say おいしかったです (oishikatta desu). With friends, おいしかった is enough.

intro: 乾杯 (kanpai) means "Cheers!" Japanese people say it together while raising their glasses at the start of a drinking party or celebration. It is also a noun for the toast itself.
literal: 乾 means "dry" and 杯 means "cup," so 乾杯 is literally "dry the cup," in other words, drink it all. Today it is just a toast, and nobody expects you to empty your glass.
usage: At a party in Japan, people usually wait until everyone has a drink. Then one person gives a short speech and leads everyone in 乾杯！ Drinking before the toast is considered bad manners.
People clink glasses and take the first sip together. You can toast with any drink, including tea, juice or water.
At work parties, people often hold their glass a little lower than a senior person's when clinking, as a small sign of respect.
Among friends, people often stretch it out cheerfully as かんぱーい！. You can also make it a verb: 乾杯しよう ("Let's toast").

faq.q: Is it kanpai or kampai?
faq.a: Both spellings are used. The Japanese is かんぱい. Standard Hepburn writes kanpai, but the ん sounds like m before p, so kampai is also common.

faq.q: Do you have to drink alcohol for kanpai?
faq.a: No. You can toast with tea, juice or water. What matters is raising your glass with everyone.

intro: お腹すいた (onaka suita) means "I'm hungry." It is the everyday way to say you want to eat, and you hear it often in anime and at home. The polite version is お腹がすきました.
literal: お is a polite prefix, 腹 means "belly," and すいた is the past form of すく, "to become empty." Literally it is "My stomach has become empty." Japanese uses the past form here to describe how you feel now.
usage: Say お腹すいた to friends and family when you are hungry. In speech, the particle が is usually dropped, but お腹がすいた is also natural.
With people you speak politely to, say お腹がすきました. To ask someone if they are hungry, say お腹すいた？ (casual) or お腹すいていますか (polite).
Men sometimes say 腹減った (hara hetta). It means the same thing but sounds rough and masculine.
To say you are very hungry, add ペコペコ: お腹ペコペコ ("I'm starving"). The opposite, "I'm full," is お腹いっぱい.

faq.q: Why is onaka suita in the past tense?
faq.a: すいた means your stomach has become empty, so it describes your current state. Japanese often uses this past form for feelings that just started, like つかれた (I'm tired).

faq.a: Say お腹がすきました (onaka ga sukimashita).
